maintopic: THE LATE RIGHT HON. ARTHUR MEIGHEN TRIBUTES ON PASSING OF FORMER PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA

speechtext:
Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime
Minister): Mr. Speaker, this morning Right Hon. Arthur Meighen passed away. In his passing Canada has lost a devoted statesman, the commonwealth one of its founding fathers, and the world of letters one of its master craftsmen. His career from his first participation in public affairs to the present spanned more than half the history of Canada since confederation. He first came into the House of Commons in 1908. He was appointed solicitor general in 1913 and -was sworn of the privy council of Canada on October 2, 1915. Later he became a member of the imperial privy council, and was twice prime minister of Canada.
It has been given to few Canadians to have served so long and made so distinguished a contribution. This is not the time to review his life or his achievements, but it can be said that the true nature of that contribution grows with the years as historical perspective makes clearer the real truth of this man and his mission, often misunderstood.
I had the opportunity some months ago of seeing him for the last time, and I could not but marvel at his attitude toward life and his freedom from recrimination whatever the vicissitudes of his life had been. Indeed, his own words displayed the nobility of this man. He said on one memorable occasion:
Fortune came and fortune fled. It is only the lot of all of us, at least of all who strive-the joy of the upward struggle, the successes, disappointments and defeats. Perhaps it has been my fate to have had more than the average on both sides of the account, but I promise you there Is going to be nothing of bitterness carried forward after the page is turned . .. Whether now judged right or wrong, whatever I have said, whatever I have done, is going to remain unrevised and unrepented .. .
The page of his great life is now turned forever. The book of our history is richer because he wrote upon that page. His life was characterized, above all, by stainless integrity, courage and steadfastness of faith. I have mentioned the honours that came to him throughout the years and I shall not
repeat them. Only one member of this house was here during the days when Arthur Meighen occupied so great a place in this forum, and that is the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe).
I heard him speak on a number of occasions, and they were unforgettable. He had the unique distinction of having been the only Canadian who had held the four great offices of parliament, for he was both prime minister and leader of the opposition in the House of Commons, and government leader and leader in opposition in the Senate. His voice was heard in adornment of 23 sessions of the House of Commons and 13 sessions of the Senate.
Arthur Meighen was my friend. I twice contested a seat in parliament under his leadership. I heard him on the hustings many times, and whenever I heard that man the words of Lord Curzon, as he described another great statesman, Right Hon. Herbert Asquith, came to mind:
Whenever I have heard him on a first rate occasion, there arose in my mind the image of some great military parade. The words, the arguments, the points, follow each other with the steady tramp of regiments across the field; each unit is in its place, the whole marching in rhythmical order; the sunlight glints on the bayonets, and ever and anon is heard the role of the drum.
Sir, he had the amazing capacity to marshall his facts and express them in language so clear and colourful that the pages of Hansard will always be a monument to his memory.
He was an outstanding scholar. From his boyhood days in St. Mary's to his last days he was immersed in the classics of the world's literature. Indeed, many of us will remember that speech on his favourite subject, Shakespeare which he delivered ex tempore, which was copious with long quotations from memory; that speech reproduced time and again in anthologies containing collections of the world's greatest speeches.
To his intimates he was a warm and sensitive personality. This was so in his latter days, but those who knew him well will also bear witness that even in his most controversial days he maintained a spirit of generous forgiveness to those who wounded; an attitude of companionship in a common dedication to those with whom he disagreed; an uncommon loyalty to his friends and followers. I think of his words regarding his predecessor in office as prime minister of

The Late Right Hon. Arthur Meighen Canada, Right Hon. Sir R. L. Borden, of whom Mr. Meighen used these words, so applicable today:
Happy indeed are they who, as the night of life approaches, find that the inner vision does not fade. Happier still are they who, as the shadows lengthen, have full assurance that they bore with head unbowed a strong man's measure of the heat and burden, who are conscious that they enjoy the undimmed confidence of everyone who shared with them their struggles and anxieties, and who have just cause to hope that when all is over there will be heard from their fellow men the simple and sincere benediction: "He served his country well".

maintopic: THE LATE RIGHT HON. ARTHUR MEIGHEN TRIBUTES ON PASSING OF FORMER PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: THE LATE RIGHT HON. ARTHUR MEIGHEN TRIBUTES ON PASSING OF FORMER PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when we heard a short time ago of the death of Mr. Meighen I think we shared with all Canadians a feeling of sorrow at the death of one of Canada's outstanding citizens; a man, as the Prime Minister has put it, of great nobility of character; a former prime minister who made a distinguished contribution in politics and in business to the development of our country and our commonwealth.
Few Canadians in all history have surpassed him in intellectual brilliance and scholarly attainment, in incisive skill in parliamentary work and, above all, in parliamentary debate. Few Canadians have ever served their country in so many fields of activity so selflessly and so well over such a long period of time. May he rest in peace as he served with honour.

maintopic: THE LATE RIGHT HON. ARTHUR MEIGHEN TRIBUTES ON PASSING OF FORMER PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with regret that members of the C.C.F. party heard of the passing this morning of Right Hon. Arthur Meighen.
Mr. Meighen, as the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition have so well pointed out, was an outstanding Canadian statesman, a man of great courage, a skilful debater, a tower in Canadian parliamentary history. His public career extended over more than half a century. It was interspersed with many victories and some defeats, but on all those occasions Mr. Meighen showed himself a master. He was an outstanding leader of the Conservative party. He was a great Canadian, and our nation will mourn this day at his passing.

maintopic: THE LATE RIGHT HON. ARTHUR MEIGHEN TRIBUTES ON PASSING OF FORMER PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, our Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition and the house leader of the C.C.F. party, the hon. member for Assiniboia, have eloquently expressed, I am sure, the sentiments of all members of this Canadian House of Commons. However, perhaps I might have permission to pay a personal tribute to one with whom I have been associated in different ways for many years.

It was my privilege, as the Prime Minister has said, to enter parliament as a member with Right Hon. Mr. Meighen in 1925. Many others who joined us on that occasion have not been so privileged as I have been with health in survival. However, this outstanding Canadian was known to those of us who were closely associated with him as many other Canadians have been known by their close associates.
His ability was legendary. He was brilliant on the floor of parliament, and in all the history of the Canadian House of Commons and Senate debates his debating skill has never been surpassed. As the Prime Minister said, he achieved many outstanding distinctions in our Canadian history.
I also feel that while his ability was legendary generally, his outstanding loyalty, statesmanship and leadership inspired all those who were close to him. Indeed his sterling political integrity and character earned the lively respect of all those who dared oppose him. I have valued very highly my close association with him through all these years to which I have referred. His friendship has been an inspiration to me and his loyalty has never been in doubt amongst his close friends.
I could add many things from the memory I have of him, but let me say to you, Mr. Speaker, and to all my associates here that I am sure I am only expressing the feelings of the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition and all members of the House of Commons when I say that Canada has lost a great Canadian, the senior privy councillor, having been sworn in in 1915. He was the oldest living ex-prime minister. His memory to me will always be an inspiration. To Mrs. Meighen and to the family I express on my own behalf, and on behalf of my family, our sympathy and high respect.

subtopic: FALL-OUT SHELTERS-PROVISION FOR INCORPORATION IN NEW HOMES

speakeroldname: Hon. D. J. Walker (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
subtopic: FALL-OUT SHELTERS-PROVISION FOR INCORPORATION IN NEW HOMES
speechtext:
I have a brief announcement to make concerning fall-out shelters. Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, at the request of the emergency measures organization, has prepared a pamphlet giving basic criteria on the method of designing a basement fall-out shelter for new housing. The pamphlet is being issued today.
Entitled "Blueprint for Survival No. 2", it is the second in a series showing survival techniques in the event of radiation fall-out. You will recall that the Prime Minister announced the first pamphlet "Blueprint for

Survival No. 1", in this house on June 17, 1960 which explained the construction of fall-out shelters in existing houses.
If they so desire, borrowers under the National Housing Act may include a fallout shelter when planning their houses and the cost of the shelter may be considered in the appraised value of the house for mortgage loan purposes. Up to $500 of additional loan will be made available to assist in the financing of an acceptable fall-out shelter in new housing built for home ownership. Where necessary, the maximum loan regulations can be exceeded by up to $500 for this purpose.
I must emphasize that the additional $500 may only be used to incorporate a fall-out shelter in a new house. Fall-out shelters for existing houses, as mentioned by the Prime Minister, may be financed with home improvement loans under the National Housing Act.

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Flynn in the chair.
217. Departmental administration, $3,212,477.

Mr. Chairman, it will be clear to the committee from the statements which have been made from this side of the house on this item that we propose to criticize, as strongly as we can, the defence policy of the government in so far as it has been submitted to us by statements from government spokesmen. Our criticism will be strong, but it is designed, notwithstanding what has already been said from the other side, to be constructive. When we advocate, as we have advocated, the scrapping of certain weapons
7600	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence and equipment, and indeed the scrapping of certain policies, because we do not think they meet the requirements of the present situation, we also propose something else which in our opinion will be more effective and more useful.
It is quite clear, Mr. Chairman, that criticism of the defence policy of the government is not confined to members of the opposition in this House of Commons. The minister said in his statement yesterday that Canadians support the commitments we have undertaken. Perhaps Canadians do support the commitments, but it is obvious from a study of the Organs of public opinion throughout the country, from articles, from editorials, that a great many Canadians do not support the way this government is undertaking to carry out its commitments. The criticism is widespread; it is general, and it has been expressed in far stronger language than any that has been used in this House of Commons.
I want to say at the beginning that any criticism from us is no reflection on our armed services, for whom we have the same admiration as that which has been expressed by spokesmen for the government. We know that our armed services will discharge, as they have in the past, with skill, with loyalty and with effectiveness and devotion any tasks which may be submitted to them. In addition, Mr. Chairman, our criticism is not aimed at the minister personally or anyone associated with the minister in the government. There is no personal reflection of any kind in what we may say. Some of us on this side, because we have had the responsibility of office, are aware of the terrific responsibility which the minister of national defence in any free country must bear in an international situation of tenseness, and uncertainty, such as exists today, and where conditions change rapidly almost from week to week and certainly from month to month.
The government through the minister, who is facing this terriffic responsibility, feel that their defence policy has been a great success. Yesterday the minister said the fact that our country continues to be secure indicates the success of their policies. He would indeed be an optimistic person, Mr. Chairman, to feel that, in the circumstances of today, our country or any other free country is secure. Surely there must be more important evidence of the success of the defence policy of the government than that, before we on this side will be impressed by that success.
So we criticize policy alone, and we recognize, as my hon. friend from Trinity said yesterday, that in our criticism we do not have all the facts of the situation. It is inevitable that the minister will have more information than we have, because there is certain


information that he cannot, for security reasons, make available to us. We recognize the fact that because of the availability to the minister of information which perhaps cannot be made available to us, criticism from this side should not only take that into consideration, not only should it be constructive, but also it may have to be revised in the light Of information which later becomes available. We base our views of defence policy on what we know, which includes what we have been told by the minister.
We have learned very little indeed in this session about defence policy, and the considerations on which it is based, except those very general considerations which are non-controversial. We had hoped from the beginning of this session that provision might be made by which we, on as non-partisan a basis as is possible, could analyse, discuss and examine defence policy in its broadest as well as its more detailed aspects, before a parliamentary defence committee called for that purpose and with terms of reference which would have made that possible.
We tried to get such a committee, Mr. Chairman, and we failed. There was a defence committee set up. It was set up initially to discuss expenditures which had been made, and only after a debate in this house were its terms of reference broadened to include the estimates before us this session. It was set up after a good deal of delay and a good deal of confusion. We suspected at the time the debate took place in this house that such a committee, with such terms of reference, would be prevented from making a real inquiry into defence policy. And it was. Our suspicions were realized. As was said in the debate setting up that committee-
By whom?

If the hon. gentleman will be patient I will quote chapter and verse to confirm what I have just said. You might save your interruptions until I have finished my arguments. The record is quite revealing in this regard, and I will quote it and put it in Hansard. I will quote first from the record of the debate in this house and then from the record of the meetings of the committee. The Minister of National Defence said on March 17 of this year, at page 2180 of Hansard, talking about the work of that committee:
To discuss that policy-
That is defence policy.
_would not be within the competence of the
committee.
Then a few minutes later on the same day, on page 2184, the minister seemed to contradict himself:

Whenever estimates are submitted to a committee or to the house in committee of the whole, policy can always be discussed.
But the Prime Minister on the same day, on page 2180, had this to say:
. . . the committee shall not discuss defence policies.
He was talking about the proposed defence committee. On the next day, March 18, the Prime Minister made it quite clear that expenditures discussed before this committee were to be considered in relation to the general policy, but that the general policy was not to be discussed. I quote what he said:
It will be up to the committee itself to decide where the dividing line between administration and policy is drawn.
That was the final reference to the work of this committee before it was set up. Let us see how the government members of the committee, the majority of the committee, drew this line between administration and policy. The committee began its meetings late in the session. The Liberal members of that committee had hoped from the beginning, and indeed expected, that expert witnesses would be called; not, of course, defence officials or serving officers, but others, for questioning on any policy matter. The subcommittee on agenda and procedures on May 11 recommended that, and I hope from its minutes-
-the witnesses at the start be restricted to the minister and the departmental officials.
Then the committee, on May 17, at page 69 of its minutes, adopted a recommendation that-[DOT]
-in the event that the committee decided to call witnesses other than officials of the department . . .
They would be heard after the minister and after the officials. Then we went on. On June 1 the subcommittee-I quote from page 183 of the minutes-
*-agreed to refer these matters-
That is, the calling of outside witnesses.
-to the main committee for determination.
The main committee agreed that after it had examined all the items in the estimates it would leave item 1 open, and I quote from its report:
-then the committee would consider the advisability of calling other witnesses.
Then we get to July 8, toward the end of the work of the committee. My hon. friend from Trinity asked:
When is it the intention of this committee to hear other witnesses, if at all, or is it true that there has never been any intention on the part of the government to allow other witnesses to appear?
Supply-National Defence
In reply to that question the chairman of the committee said the matter would be discussed by the steering committee; and the final action of the committee, on July 19, was to ask the steering committee to consider again the calling of outside witnesses and report back "with reasonable dispatch". Then this question was resolved by a majority vote of the committee not to call any at all.
I ask you, Mr. Chairman, if that was not stalling by the majority on the committee, to give an impression that witnesses might be called, without any intention of permitting them to be called.
Hear, hear.

In any event, they were not called and there was no opportunity of examining anyone on defence policy, except the minister. What opportunities did members of the committee itself have to examine defence policy and put forward ideas to the government? Practically none.
You were not there.

I have read every page of the minutes of proceedings of every meeting of the committee, and all you have to do is read the record and see what happened. I will put some of it on Hansard. On page 326 the chairman of the committee had this to say, and I quote from the record, underlining my statement that we could merely ask questions and not discuss policy:
All I wanted to tell you, Mr. Hellyer, is that if there is no money included in the 1960-61 estimates, then we are not going to ask the minister any questions about that at all.
That was even a restriction on questions. Then at page 327 of the same day's meeting the chairman said this:
If there is not any money included in those estimates for nuclear warheads, I do not see how we can ask questions about this.
At page 330 in the report of the same meeting Mr. Hellyer said this:
All you have to do is say it is the policy of this government that both these weapons will be equipped with nuclear weapons, or they will not be.
What did the chairman say to that?
Bring that up next year ... We are not spending money on it now.
Again, at page 352, the chairman said:
All we are doing here is going through the estimates of 1960-61 in which there is no money provided for psychological warfare, and therefore any questions are out of order.
Then he said to the member for Burin-Burgeo, who had brought this question up, or tried to bring it up:
Have you another field?
And Mr. Carter replied:
It has to do with ideological warfare.

Supply-National Defence
As perhaps the warfare we are facing in the world today is even more ideological than military, the hon. member thought it might be suitable in the defence committee to make some reference to this fact. But the chairman said:
We are not spending any money on that either, so that is out of order.
On page 383 the hon. member for Trinity began to question the minister on the problem of defence and its relation to national sovereignty. Surely that would be a subject suitable for discussion in this defence committee. The parliamentary secretary to the minister said:
There is no item on sovereignty, Mr. Chairman.
Then the chairman said:
No, X was going to suggest that after the session is all over, we all get together and have a picnic and ask questions then.
Then on page 497 of the minutes the chairman said:
Would you please ask direct questions and not make so many comments ... Leave off the statements.
That, Mr. Chairman, is how defence policy was analysed, examined and discussed in the defence expenditures committee of this house. So we did not get very far in our discussion of defence policy. What then is the position now in this regard?
We have been left completely in the dark, in the record of the committee certainly, in respect of such important matters as nuclear testing and the use of nuclear weapons by Canadian forces. There was very little if anything done is this defence committee to elucidate the position of the government in these matters, though there was something done, I confess, to register the existing confusion in regard to them.
Let us look at nuclear testing for the moment. Government policy, as we see it, is one of shifting and changing. This has already been discussed in this house. The Prime Minister laid down the policy of the government in this matter on August 22, 1958, in words which have already been put on the record, at page 3944 of Hansard for that year:
The house will recall that on several occasions since I became Prime Minister I have advocated the suspension of nuclear tests, but always providing there was adequate international control to ensure the observance of the undertakings made in that connection.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs repeated what he had said earlier when on February 9, 1960, as reported at page 866 of Hansard, he said:
Our position is very clear, Mr. Speaker; we are against further nuclear tests, period.


If that is not a contradiction between positions I do not know what is. But when I questioned the Prime Minister in regard to this contradiction and tried to get it resolved in order that we would know where we stood on such matters of vital importance, the Prime Minister said:
I see no contradiction in the viewpoint expressed today and that expressed two years ago, except that naturally with the events that are now taking place modifications become necessary in order to meet changing conditions. Possibly what I have said should not be considered as a modification. What it is in fact is an interpretation of an actual reality existing today.
I was there quoting the Prime Minister, as reported on page 2252 of Hansard for this year. That is meant to mean, presumably, that the Prime Minister had altered his position from August, 1958 and had now joined the Secretary of State for External Affairs in coming out against nuclear tests, period.
Not long after, on June 4, 1960, the Prime Minister associated himself with the President of the United States in a communique which said:
Particular attention was paid to the importance of achieving, with effective international control, an end to nuclear testing-
The Secretary of State for External Affairs said that represented no change, and the Prime Minister said that represented no change. When the Prime Minister was questioned on it a couple of days after the communique he said, as reported on page 4599 of Hansard:
We have made it very clear that we believe in the complete termination of nuclear testing.
It was not made very clear in a document so important as a communique which was signed by the President of the United States and the Prime Minister of Canada. Apparently, notwithstanding this communique -because we base our views not on this statement but on decisions made in this house- the government now rejects any form of nuclear testing even under international control and agreement; even if it is for nonmilitary purposes, such as has been proposed for the Alberta tar sands; even if there were no fall-out, such as would be the case in an underground test, and even if it were under United Nations or other form of international control.
If that is the position of the government, that position should be made clear outside Canada as it is meant to be made clear inside Canada. I am not questioning that position taken by the government, but to take such a categorical, unqualified position, if that is what it is, while at the same time accepting nuclear weapons which could not be brought to their peak of efficiency without testing,

would be inconsistent with the policy of the government in regard to testing to the point of hypocrisy.
Nothing of the kind, and you know better.
I repeat what I have said.
That will not make it any more powerful.

I will put it on the record again. To say in one breath "We are against nuclear testing, period" and in another "We will use nuclear weapons" which obviously cannot be brought to the utmost of efficiency without testing, is inconsistent.
What is the justification for the latter part of the statement? That they have not done sufficient testing now so that nuclear weapons and their potency can be established?

The answer to that should be obvious to anyone; that nuclear weapons, when they are ready for use, have been brought to that position as the result of nuclear testing. The Prime Minister is against nuclear testing, but we will perhaps use nuclear weapons.
Let us see if we can find out the position of the government with regard to this other related matter, the use of nuclear weapons. On June 23 before the defence expenditures committee, as reported on page 323 of the report, the Minister of National Defence said this:
The Bomarc anti-aircraft missile to be effective would require nuclear weapons.
That statement, of course, has been confirmed by many United States experts and military authorities, most recently by the general commanding NORAD. The Prime Minister made the same kind of statement on February 20, 1959 page 1223 of Hansard for that year, which I think was quoted last night by the minister. The Prime Minister said:
The full potential of these defensive weapons is achieved only when they are armed with nuclear warheads.
Before the defence committee, page 294 of the report, the minister said with reference to another weapon:
When the Honest John-
Not "if" the Honest John.
-is supplied which will be a year from now, then our forces will have a nuclear capability.
I assume no one would wish to have a weapon in the Canadian forces which was not of maximum effectiveness, and as the Bomarc can only be of maximum effectiveness if it has nuclear warheads, so we are
Supply-National Defence told, then if the Bomarc is supplied it would be supplied for use in certain circumstances with nuclear warheads. Indeed, it is difficult to conceive of any circumstance where a weapon would be used without its maximum effectiveness.
Who will control this nuclear capability? The minister made that perfectly clear before the defence expenditures committee. As reported on page 312 of the report he said:
My understanding is that the authority has to come from the President of the United States before nuclear weapons are used. These warheads belong to the United States. That permission having been granted to Canada to use these weapons, then the decision is made by Canada as to whether or not she will take advantage of that permission given by the United States.
Later in the same meeting he said, page 313 of the report:
I can only give this to you in general terms. The nuclear weapons cannot be used until they are released by the President of the United States. They then would be released to the supreme allied commander in Europe.
On this occasion the minister was talking about nuclear weapons with NATO forces on the continent, I believe. Later, again at the same meeting, page 322 of the report, quoting the Prime Minister the minister said:
We cannot change the principle of United States ownership.
Then the minister went on, page 331 of the report:
If those disarmament conferences are not successful, then we may, as the Prime Minister said, require those weapons to be used by Canadian forces.
I think we have the right to conclude from this and other statements which have been made, Mr. Chairman, that the situation with regard to actual use is somewhat fluid at the present time. Indeed, that was the word used by the minister, I think in the committee; that the situation was fluid at the present time. Well, if it is fluid-and I think that is the minimum expression which could be used-are there negotiations going on with regard to this matter which may clear up these difficulties? Yes; or no; or perhaps; depending upon which statement you read. In February, 1959 the Prime Minister, as reported on page 1223 of Hansard-I think the minister quoted this yesterday in his statement too-said this:
The government is, therefore, examining with the United States government questions connected with the acquisition of nuclear warheads for Bomarc and other defensive weapons...
We are confident that we shall be able to reach formal agreement with the United States on appropriate means to serve the common objective.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs, following a question I asked him in the committee on external affairs as to whether

Supply-National Defence negotiations were still going on with the United States government on the use of nuclear weapons and their control by Canadian authorities, said:
There has been no agreement on that... I am not in a position to make any report on that at the moment... Certain negotiations are underway. but I think not on the particular point you mention.
That extract is to be found at page 73. of the report of the committee on external affairs. In other words, the Secretary of State for External Affairs said there were negotiations going on, but only, he added, in respect of the storage of nuclear weapons; that is, the storage of United States nuclear weapons on Canadian soil. On page 73 of the report of the committee I added:
-and there are no negotiations going on in respect of this supposed change of policy at all.
I was referring there to the use by Canada of nuclear weapons. The Secretary of State for External Affairs replied:
No. There are discussions going on, off and on, between the various allies in NATO.
Is it surprising that we on this side are in some confusion as to what is actually happening in regard to the negotiations on such a vital matter as the use and control of nuclear weapons? When the Minister of National Defence used the word "negotiations" with regard to the storage of such weapons by the United States at Goose Bay, which is territory leased by the United States, he apparently meant, because he made that clear in the committee, political negotiations leading to an agreement. When he used the word "negotiations" or "discussions" regard-ind the use of nuclear weapons by Canadian forces, presumably he meant something very different, and this is one source of our confusion.
The minister said as reported on page 327 .of the minutes of the defence expenditures committee, referring to negotiations with the United States:
These negotiations regarding nuclear weapons have not been pressed very urgently because we have no Bomarcs yet.
And again, as reported on page 333, he said:
We have not got to the stage of exchanging notes regarding any other of the nuclear weapons. However, talks have been going on between officials and ministers on the matter.
He was questioned by the hon. member for Calgary South on this point, as follows:
You would have discussions at the service level followed by cabinet discussions where a policy decision would be arrived at by the cabinet as a whole-

Then the hon. member added this:
Then the Department of External Affairs at the diplomatic level would exchange notes. Is this the complete sequence?
To which the minister for defence replied, yes. In other words, on the evidence we have before us, on the statements made, negotiations in this field which is of such vital political as well as military importance, becomes a matter for the Department of External Affairs only when the stage of exchanging notes is reached. Presumably the Secretary of State for External Affairs agrees with that, because he has already told us in this house, and he reported to the committee, that he was not participating in any such negotiations.
Well, Mr. Chairman, you know what I mean when I say this matter seems to have been left in the air. We bring in those responsible for foreign policy only when the formal notes have to be exchanged. That is made clear in the report of the committee on the defence estimates. So I ask, could there be greater confusion anywhere, or could there be a more important measure on which to be confused than this? I suggest that this confusion was made even worse by the minister's statement yesterday when he mentioned the matter, as reported on page 7557 of Hansard, as follows:
We are, therefore, going ahead with the procurement of the vehicles which can use these nuclear weapons, but the decision as to the acquisition of nuclear warheads depends on circumstances which might develop some time in the future.
So we are going ahead with the preparation of facilities for the use of nuclear weapons; we are preparing for the possibility of using nuclear weapons, but we have not as yet made a decision, according to the minister, as to whether or not we shall use them or, if we do, on what conditions shall govern their control. At the present time, unless the situation has changed as a result of diplomatic negotiation and agreement, such weapons cannot be used by any Canadian force except by agreement with the President of the United States. That is the situation with regard to this matter and I suggest it is a very unsatisfactory situation indeed.
What should be our policy with regard to these matters? What do we on this side think our policy should be? Following what my hon. friend from Trinity said yesterday, I should like to put forward in a general way-because it can only be done in a general way at this time-some views, some recommendations, on defence policy and its relationship to foreign policy as we see it on this side of the house.
It is a time, we think, for radical change in our defence policy. It is not a time for

weakening our defences. It is certainly no time for wasting our money and for drifting along without a policy. Especially for a country like Canada it is a time for reexamination from the ground up of what we are doing, a re-examination in the light of strategic developments going back to the day three years ago when the Russians threw their first missile into outer space and thereby the whole concept of strategy was changed in as revolutionary a way as it was by the invention of gunpowder. It is a time to re-examine our policy in the light of the western coalition which has also changed in recent years; to re-examine it in the light of our resources, and to re-examine it in the light of our national interest. When I talk about the national interest I am not thinking of the short range, selfish national interest but of the long range national interests, the paramount one of which is to help maintain the peace, to help build up a coalition, a genuine coalition, as a basis for collective security, collective welfare and collective progress and to give a lead to other middle powers in the achievement of those objectives.
I agree with the Minister of National Defence when he said, though he perhaps did not use these words, that narrow nationalism will not do today. There can in my view be no neutralism for Canada in defence or foreign policy. I have been getting a good deal of correspondence, and no doubt so has the minister, on this question of whether we should disengage ourselves from the western coalition, and whether we could not play a more important and constructive role by virtue of such disengagement by moving in the direction of what has been called neutralism. A good deal of the comment which I get in the letters I receive is based on Mr. Minifie's book. I have replied to these letters, and perhaps I can put some of my words on the record:
I agree with a great deal of what Mr. Minifie says in his book. I certainly believe we should reexamine our defence relations with the United States, and indeed our foreign policy generally in the light of some of the considerations which he puts forward.
I cannot, however, go as far as he does in advocating that Canada should dissociate herself completely from the North Atlantic coalition and substitute for the present policy of collective action and collective security one of neutralism without any commitments except to the United Nations. The reason why I cannot go so far as that is because the inference would inevitably and reasonably be drawn from such a policy that our relations with the United States and the U.S.S.R. should be on the same level of interest and responsibility; indeed, that there was nothing to choose, so far as Canadian defence policy was concerned, between our two powerful neighbours.
I know that there are faults, and some dangers, in U.S. policy, but I think also that there is a
Supply-National Defence basic difference between the principles that underlie its policy and those which determine that of the communist imperialist system of the Soviet union. Recognizing, as I do, that difference, I cannot believe that abandonment of our present policies for complete neutrality would be a constructive step in the interest of peace. I think that we should continue to associate ourselves as closely as possible with the United States, the United Kingdom, France and other North Atlantic countries but that we should direct all of our activities and policy inside this association to the maintenance and strengthening of peace and the ending of the cold war in a way which would make the present system of defence through huge armaments unnecessary.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I believe as much as I have ever believed in collective action, especially in world collective action through the United Nations. I believe more than ever, in orienting our defence policy more than ever in the direction of having ready, trained and equipped forces for United Nations service; yet I feel that genuine collective action in these matters-and I am thinking more particularly of NATO-is more difficult now than it was 10 years ago when NATO was born, born in fear and apprehension.
Furthermore, I am sure the minister knows we have to so organize our collective forces now that they will take the shock of the all important first days, or even the first hours, of any nuclear war. In world war III, if we are mad enough to allow it to begin, as contrasted with world wars I and II there will be no time to learn from experience; our survival will depend on what we have planned, on what we have organized and what we have done up to that moment, not likely on anything we may do subsequently. And what we have done up to that moment will be our only hope for survival if we lose the only real defence which now exists, which is defence by the maintenance of peace.
I suggest we should not forget, as we are now being subjected to some reassuring statements from certain quarters-I wish they could be realistic; I wish that they impressed me as being realistic-about the possibility of living through a nuclear war, because it has a bearing on this kind of thing; that one single bomb today can harbour a destructive force greater than all the energy ever used in any form to fight all the wars in history before 1939. But also, and this is a corollary to that horrible idea, let us not in our defence or our foreign policy become the prisoners of the forces that this awful situation may provoke.
It is on that basis, on those principles-I would like to call them that-that I have tried to work out my own views as to what our defence policy should be at this time. I admit at once that it is not easy to do that, and it has taken two or three years of what

Supply-National Defence has been referred in another context as agonizing reappraisal before one could put views forward, so far as I am concerned; and I do not put them forward as anything final and fixed that could not be changed. They may even have to be changed, if we knew all the information that the minister has at his disposal as opposed to the information I have at my disposal.
But these are my views. Indeed most of them were also put forward yesterday by the hon. member for Trinity. So far as continental defence is concerned-I start with that first-I repeat what my hon. friend said. In my view we should get out of the whole SAGE-Bomarc operation, and we should not spend any more money on radar gap fillers. Our objection to the Bomarc is not only that we do not think it is an effective weapon. I admit that its tests lately have been certainly far more successful than the previous tests. Perhaps for certain purposes it may become an effective weapon, I do not know; but that is not our major objection to it. Our objection is to the kind of defence strategy it represents and which we do not think will be effective however effective the weapon may be. If the United States wishes to continue that kind of protection, let the United States do so. Let us withdraw from that direct form of continental defence.
After all, this kind of defence is primarily a United States responsibility. It is the defence of the deterrent. We know how important that is; but it is a deterrent which is under the sole control of the United States of America. It is not a defence, and in the nature of things I submit cannot be a defence, of our territory in the traditional sense of the word, and it will soon be no defence of anything. As the minister himself has indicated, in a few years missile attack will make this kind of defence of very minimal importance indeed, once missiles supersede airborne bombers, and that will not be long from now.
It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that our experience in the last three years has shown that in attempting to participate in continental defence in the way we have, we are becoming, nothing more than just the last two knots on the Bomarc tail of the defence kite. I believe that in getting out of this position, which I consider to be an ineffective one for Canada, we would be rejecting the use by us of any form of nuclear weapons for what is mistakenly called the defence of our territory. I believe, however, that we should continue the part we are now playing in early warning operations, though they will be of diminishing importance as new methods of missile attack are developed.


To meet these new methods of attack by intercontinental ballistic missiles, the United States has very far-reaching, very expensive plans for ballistic missile early warning systems. I believe that we in Canada should accept no responsibility for the construction or operation of new warning systems against intercontinental missiles. I think this is out of our league and we should not become involved in it. I am not suggesting we are; I do not think we are at the moment, but I suggest we should keep out of it.
This brings up the whole question of what should be our defence relationship with the United States; what should be our attitude toward United States requests for Canada's co-operation in carrying out certain defence policies which are primarily in the interest of the United States, perhaps in the protection of the deterrent but in that sense these, of course, are in the general interest because anything that is in the interest of the United States as far as protection is concerned naturally is in the interest of every member of the coalition. If the United States goes, the coalition as we know it falls.
The hon. member for Trinity also dealt with this matter in terms of the role that in our view should be played by our Canadian air defence squadrons. We think, I repeat, that role should be limited to one of recognition and identification, with new planes which will be effective for that purpose and which will, if this role is accepted, result in a reduction in our squadrons, we think, by about one half, because not more than four or five squadrons would be required for this new role. The hon. member pointed out yesterday that it would also, we hope, make possible the exchange of these new planes purchased from the United States for the CL-44 made in Canada, an arrangement which the government is attempting at the moment, I understand, to bring about. This change in our continental defence policy would, as I say, permit us to reduce the number of existing air defence CF-100 squadrons perhaps by one half; in any event the CF-lOO's would not be effective even in this role of recognition and identification, because they would not be able to fly high enough or fast enough.
In certain other aspects of our continental relationship with the United States-and it is unfortunate that they are all outside NATO-I believe we are tied to a greater extent than ever before in our history to United States plans, to United States control and to United States strategy. I think we should begin the process of reversing this position, as we do in the proposals which we make in this debate, and that we should do our best to ensure that close co-operation,

which is essential, does not mean being swallowed up by the Pentagon, which is not.
I do not want that to be interpreted to mean that we should repudiate the obligation of our membership in the western alliance. It does not mean either, of course, that we can ignore the compulsions of geography or the requirements of collective security in a dangerous, cold war world. We must co-operate with the United States, but there is no reason why we should not reexamine the nature of our co-operation, the basis of that co-operation, and divert that co-operation into ways which we believe to be sensible for us without being too sensitive or touchy about our own separate rights and sovereignty and all that kind of thing.
If, for instance, the United States needs, and if it can satisfy us that the need is justified, certain facilities on Canadian soil, and if we cannot or do not desire for reasons which seem good to us to ourselves provide these facilities and the services that go with them, then I do not think we should refuse to make the necessary political agreement with our neighbour, as has been done in the United Kingdom. But they should be in clear terms which will always recognize our own sovereign right of ultimate control.
If such an agreement were to extend to the use of air bases in Canada, as is the case in the United Kingdom, although the agreement there is under reconsideration at the present time, I suggest that any such agreement for the use of Canadian bases, and I think this is important, should only be on the condition that we have complete information about every United States flight from every such Canadian base, and that we have a veto over every such flight off that base if we consider it necessary on policy grounds.
I will say only a word about the army side of our defence policy, but it is a word which I think underlines something of importance, and I have no doubt that the minister will agree with me in principle. We should make a brigade in Canada air transportable and trained and equipped for the United Nations and other international peace and police force purposes. On this subject may I say that I know arrangements have been made, I think as effectively in this country as in any other country that is a member of the United Nations, so that forces can be made available for the kind of United Nations police activity which is now going on in the Congo. But surely the experience of the Suez and now the experience of the Congo have shown that what seem to be required most from us for these purposes are not combatant but technical, administrative and staff troops. While I understand that we
Supply-National Defence have a battalion trained and ready now and equipped with transport for this kind of duty, it is not our battalion which has been called on twice but rather specialized troops, signallers, administrative troops and so on. I think it would be wise for us to extend the commitments we have undertaken to the training and equipping of other Canadian troops than a battalion for this kind of service, and that we should have men trained and ready for this kind of work and equipped with the planes to transport them wherever they may be needed. No nuclear weapons are needed for this kind of important and constructive peace operation.
Then, Mr. Chairman, I wish to say a word about the necessity of modernizing the equipment of our forces for the jobs they have to do, what they have to do at present and what they may have to do in the future. My colleague the hon. member for Trinity had a good deal to say about this. I think the evidence shows that we are not in a very good situation with regard to equipment. The CF-100 is only one example. The CF-100's are kept now merely because the government has not yet been able to make up its mind what to do with them and how to replace them, though they are admittedly obsolete for the kind of interception work which would be required of them if war broke out. How are we going to re-equip our forces with modern equipment from existing appropriations so they can do the kind of job we may want them to do, and in view of the commitments for fixed expenditures with respect to other things than equipment? A well informed Canadian commentator on defence policy, Wing Commander Gellner, writing in Saturday Night on February 20 quoted the minister as saying:
I960 is perhaps the year in which we could pause in our defence spending for armaments.
If the minister was reported correctly I suppose he meant equipment, modernization and that kind of thing. I do not think the minister would agree, in view of what he said yesterday, that there is much likelihood of a pause in that regard in the immediate future. Perhaps he was not accurately quoted, although that is the sentence that appears in the article. In any event, whether or not we are pausing, and I do not believe we are pausing in that field, how is the minister going to find the resources for this essential work of re-equipment when so much of the present appropriation goes toward personnel costs, operations and maintenance, so much indeed that comparatively little is now left over for the new equipment which is essential?

Under category 2, operation and maintenance, the figure is $631,935,000; and under category 3, equipment, the figure is $360,237,000. It is going to be difficult-perhaps the minister may say it is impossible-to reduce the amounts to be spent on the first two categories. Indeed, under recent conditions, with pay increases and all that kind of thing, they are going up. So with the same budget the amount available for equipment goes down at a time when so much new equipment is essential if we are to continue our present policy and discharge our obligations under it.
Indeed, the present trend, with the first two categories going up and the third category going down, means, if you project that trend, that by 1964-65 we shall be spending almost $700 million on personnel costs and $800 million on operation and maintenance, which would leave practically nothing for equipment. In an editorial in Saturday Night of February 20, the date on which the article appeared to which I have referred, there is the following comment:
II we are going to out down our defence spending and apportion the money as we have been doing for the past six years, by 1965 we shall have the best fed, best housed, best paid defence force in the world, with not one modern weapon, plane or ship for them to use.
Perhaps that is a little exaggerated.
Who said that?
What is the answer? Let us hear it.

I am trying to give an answer by suggesting that we should make a drastic re-examination of present defence policies. Perhaps there will be ways in which money can be saved or, if not, perhaps a reapportionment of the existing appropriations can be brought about in some way. That is the responsibility of the government, which has all the information at its disposal.
I will make one positive suggestion to the minister in regard to a reorganization of the forces which might save some money. I suggest that the present circumstances of defence require a new look, not so much a new look but some action to ensure that our defence forces operate as an integral machine. This is a matter which was very
rMr. Pearson.]

dear to the heart of the minister when he was on this side, and it should be proceeded with now for the sake of both efficiency and economy. I suggest that the present set-up is out of date, each service with a large overhead and operating independently, with a chiefs of staff committee presided over by a chairman. This is no reflection on the personnel of our present organization or the way it has been conducted because the minister knows, as I know, how efficiently that has been done by the chiefs of staff and by the chairman whose services-I am thinking of General Foulkes-have been invaluable over the years in the operation of this particular piece of defence organization.
I suggest to the minister that the time has come to change this organization for one chief of staff whose authority would extend to the three services, army, navy and air force, and perhaps defence research. He would have the chief responsibility for the planning and implementing of defence policy submitted to him by the government. In that kind of set-up the present chief of staff would be replaced by commanders for each of the services who would not be responsible for policy recommendations but for carrying out the policies and plans referred to them by, if I may call him that, the supreme chief of staff.
I think there should be also a complete integration of the administration of the three services along the lines the minister used to put forward. I suggest to the minister also that he should appoint a committee of three representative retired service officers for each of the services, perhaps ex-chiefs of staff, to make recommendations on how this integration of the three services could most speedily and effectively be brought about.
There is only one other aspect of defence about which I want to talk at this time, Mr. Chairman, and that is our position in NATO, the Canadian forces in NATO, a matter of importance and, I know, of difficulty and complexity. In my view, the situation here is not any more satisfactory than it is in respect of this continent. We are told that a re-examination is now going on of the role of NATO in the years ahead. I agree, as one who has had some experience with these things and knows something about this kind of examination, that it would not be wise to make any final determination at this time- by "final determination" I mean a final determination of our views on this side of Canada's place in NATO defence policy-until that examination is complete and we know the result of it. Pending such an examination, which I hope will be completed soon, it seems to me quite obvious that the time

has come for NATO to insist on genuine collective defence arrangements, all-out and all-embracing, in which the European members will play their full part.
When I say that, I recall to the committee the words-which I must say shocked me at the time-of the Secretary of State for External Affairs to the effect that only two members of NATO were fulfilling their commitments, Canada and the United States. I think the minister was questioned about that in the defence committee, but he did not express any particular opinion one way or the other. If this is the case, and that is what the Secretary of State for External Affairs says, then surely the time has come when all members of NATO should fulfil the commitments they have undertaken, and that NATO should become a genuine collective security organization with balanced collective forces, toward the maintenance of which each member should make its appropriate contribution. If that is not done, then NATO is not likely to survive and we know that could be a major tragedy.
I believe in particular, and this matter has been referred to, that NATO must now become strong enough to provide a non-nuclear deterrent. In the operation of that nonnuclear deterrent-deterrent by conventional weapons-I myself do not shrink from the necessity of examining the specific implications of that in considering some form of disengagement. This is something that a lot of highly qualified and highly respectable people have been considering over the years, including Sir Anthony Eden. It is almost 11 years now, I think that NATO was formed. The shield forces and their organization were developed on the assumption that the "sword" was the nuclear retaliatory force, under non-NATO control, and that it was all-powerful, which it was at that time.
This situation changed radically and finally when the Soviet union developed the capability for nuclear retaliation. In some respects at least, perhaps in missile capability, the capacity of the Soviet union is possibly greater than that of the United States. So we have these two giants facing each other with a retaliatory capacity that can destroy them both, and destroy the world in the process. That is what we call the nuclear deterrent. I am not suggesting we dispose of it because, in the present circumstances, it is certainly a foundation for that kind of uneasy peace which we have. If it did not exist we would be in a far worse condition than we are today.
However, that development, the development of Soviet nuclear retaliatory forces, must have had or certainly should have had a fundamental effect on NATO strategy. It is

The best solution would be a combination of both of those. I hope, therefore, that in-
I wonder if the Leader of the Opposition could amplify that last remark* that NATO should free itself from the retaliatory force.

Yes. I was just going to try to do that, though I do not want to spend too much time on it because I have already taken more time than I should have and the committee has been generous. I hope NATO will do what it can to free itself from reliance to such a great extent on these retaliatory forces of the United States by building up its own NATO deterrent forces which will mean, as I see it, not so much reliance on tactical nuclear weapons as on the development of those conventional forces, which the NATO experts certainly had in mind when they set the goals at Lisbon some years back. I am not suggesting that the NATO European countries will be able to meet those goals now. I suspect they cannot, but they can do a good deal more in that direction than they have done.
However, they are not likely to do this if their reliance is mainly on two things, the United States deterrent retaliatory force, which is outside their control but which is the effective deterrent at the moment, or if they rely too much on tactical nuclear weapons inside NATO forces, which may seem to be a fairly easy way out for them and relieve them from some of the responsibility of building up conventional forces.
Are you suggesting that NATO should develop this type of deterrent, or any nuclear deterrent?

No, I am not suggesting that NATO should develop anything in the nature of a strategic retaliatory force. I am suggesting that NATO-and of course I am not alone in this suggestion; every commentator on NATO military tactics and strategy is talking about it now-should develop a conventional force deterrent, which would do two things. It would cause any possible aggressor to hesitate before starting what he thought might be a local war. It might almost be a temptation to start a local aggression, if he hoped he could get away with it because the only retaliation against it might be the use of the strategic deterrent, and the President of

Supply-National Defence the United States in Washington is going to be very careful before he puts that into operation, because it means world war.
If NATO had a stronger conventional force it might serve as a very useful deterrent in that sense, I also hope that this emphasis- if that is the right word-on NATO tactical nuclear weapons will not be at the expense of building up the NATO conventional force. I am encouraged in that view by the fact that it is becomingly increasingly clear from what I read, including the most recent book by a great military expert, Captain Liddell Hart, that there is no security in these nuclear weapons-I am talking of tactical nuclear weapons-which would compensate for the danger and the possible general devastation which is inherent in their use.
I mean by that, and the minister himself has expressed this view, that if small tactical nuclear weapons are used there is the inescapable probability-some people would call it the inescapable certainty-of a deadly progression, a chain reaction from a nuclear bullet right through to a hydrogen bomb, which would destroy us all.
The minister quoted something I said in July, 1959, as to the use of these tactical nuclear weapons in NATO. I confess to him that I have changed my mind since I made that statement. I have changed my mind for three reasons. One is that I am impressed by the fact that tactical nuclear weapons will not give us the amount of tactical security which I thought might be possible then; also because I am afraid the concentration of tactical nuclear weapons under United States control-they may be given to Germany at the same time and be in German hands, but under United States control-may mean the European states will be less likely to build up defence forces which those European countries should perhaps have. Also, I am impressed by the fact that the use of these tactical nuclear weapons, even on the smallest scale, might result in radio fall-out, which would be disastrous. I have had no definite final advice on that, but I come to that conclusion in the light of the information I have been able to gather.
I confess that my views have changed since last July on the use of tactical weapons by NATO.
If I understand your suggestion correctly, this would involve increased manpower and, I suppose, Canadian manpower?

No, it would not, so far as Canada is concerned. In my view I am not sure that a very great increase in manpower would be involved, but I will come to that later. I say in any event that Canada should


categorically reject the proposition that her NATO forces should be equipped with nuclear weapons of any kind indeed; not only Canadian NATO forces, but all NATO forces should reject this proposition that there should be nuclear weapons of any kind under exclusive national control, whether it is the control of the country using them-which might be France, which has them now or will have them-or the control of another country supplying them. No NATO forces should be equipped with tactical nuclear weapons at all in those circumstances. I have not come out finally and unconditionally against such prohibition, because this re-examination is going on. But if NATO forces are to be equipped with tactical nuclear weapons at all, until some international agreement is reached outlawing these weapons completely, I suggest that this should be done only as the result of a collective NATO decision taken on the highest political level of the council, a decision which would also provide for collective NATO control and use. I can appreciate the minister's position at once by saying that I also know how difficult that will be. Has there been any such decision? Apparently not, because the minister would only say, when asked about this in the committee-and I am not criticizing him; perhaps he was not in a position to give any further information-and I quote from page 314:
I think, in general principle, the possible use of atomic weapons, in the event of attack, has been recognized by the NATO council.
That is a very careful statement, which indicates that no final decision has yet been made. Until such a final decision has been made by NATO on the highest political level, in my view Canada should not even consider equipping her European NATO forces with any kind of nuclear weapon.
If the NATO council does not take any decision on this matter, or if it takes a decision which we would consider unsatisfactory, then the big decision would have to be made by Canada whether her NATO forces could play a useful and appropriate role with conventional arms alone, or whether they should not be given some other defence assignment which would be more effective in the collective and international effort to safeguard and promote security.
Whatever that decision may ultimately be, I agree 100 per cent with what the hon. member for Trinity said yesterday, that we should not have our air division in Europe equipped with aircraft, the CF-104, carrying, not under collective control but under United States control, what has been referred to as a baby nuclear bomb in a strike attack role.
Mr. Chairman, whatever the ultimate decision by NATO about nuclear weapons, and

whatever the Canadian response to that decision-and I know that political as well as military considerations are involved in that response-I think, and I repeat, that we should not have our forces in Europe equipped with nuclear weapons until it is made.
May I say in conclusion, Mr. Chairman, that it will be clear from what I have already said that I am advocating a new approach in the field of defence policy, a new orientation, a change of direction. I am advocating not a weakening, as I see it, but a strengthening of Canada's defence policy and of its participation in the search for an enduring peace which, after all, is the only defence policy that really means anything in the long run. If we lose the peace and slide into nuclear war-because we are more likely to slide into nuclear war than to get into it in any other way-then no other form of defence is going to save us, essential though those forms may be at the present time.
I think this change of direction which I have mentioned should always have in mind the desirability of preparing our forces on land, on sea and in the air for international service, preferably under the United Nations, and getting out of nuclear armament completely, without getting out of our collective commitments. I think that is the best role for a middle power like Canada. I think it can be carried out without falling into any false illusions or neutralism or anything like that, and without defaulting on our commitments. I think that role will assist Canada in discharging an independent and constructive foreign policy, which the government talks a good deal about these days.
The minister accused us last night of suggesting nothing but scrap. Scrap, scrap, scrap; that was all, he said. I suggest to the minister that the government would be well advised to scrap its present defence policy for something better along the lines we have proposed, or along better lines if the minister can find better lines. If the government does scrap its present policy, or lack of policy, if it does disappear I suggest that it will disappear unwept, unhonoured and unsung.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to unduly take up the time of this committee, but this afternoon we have heard the Leader of the Opposition and some others make reference to the need for Canadian technical personnel for situation such as the one we have today in the Congo. Without detracting in any way from the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition, I would like to say that for some time now I have been giving considerable thought to the creation of a unit which, for want of a better name, might be called either a Canadian task force for peace or a Canadian rescue force.
I would now like to elaborate on my suggestion. As a matter of fact, Mr. Chairman, I was prepared to place my suggestion before this committee last night, but as the Associate Minister of National Defence spoke at that time I have had to wait until this opportunity. There are a number of reasons for my suggestion. The first is that Canada has one army battalion earmarked for service with the United Nations. We are advised by the minister that there are sufficient aircraft to airlift this battalion, and that it is ready for instantaneous action.
The second reason is that Canadian soldiers have amassed extensive experience serving under the auspices of the United Nations, and our soldiers are generally accepted because they are not regarded as belonging to a major power.
The third reason, Mr. Chairman-and I think this is the most important reason-is that all emergencies do not necessarily call for military intervention. I have in mind examples like earthquakes, floods, epidemics and forest fires. I would therefore suggest that the minister consider the advisability of creating or earmarking another battalion which would be able to meet emergencies such as I have enumerated. If the minister feels that the earmarking or the creation of such a unit from the existing army establishments would strain our resources, then I suggest that the government create a volunteer


civilian force on a stand-by basis. We now have a large number of civilians trained in rescue operations, and if we were to ask for volunteers we might get a favourable response.
I think we should send out a questionnaire to doctors, engineers, teachers, technicians and other skilled personnel and find out if we have in our midst the skilled personnel who would be willing to serve with such a Canadian group. This questionnaire would give us the names of persons whom we could contact quickly in an emergency. We need not have a large unit; but if the reaction were favourable we could bring these people together at the civil defence college at Arn-prior, where they could be trained to serve as a unit. A shake-down period is not only valuable but necessary.
I believe, Mr. Chairman, that there has been a proven need for such a unit, which might also include elements of the navy and air force. As an example of that need, we can recall that in one of the two recent major earthquake disasters Canada made a generous contribution of food and supplied other services. Without detracting in any way from the generosity of the gift from the Canadian government, I wonder if our contribution might not have been better remembered if we had sent a unit which was capable of conducting rescue operations. Speaking for myself, if the members of my family were buried under the debris of an earthquake I would forever remember those who worked shoulder to shoulder with me in trying to rescue my family. At such a time trained rescue workers backed by the necessary equipment would be of great assistance instead of a supply of clothing and food, however important those items may be at a later stage of the rescue operations.
Our army personnel and certain selected civilians are now receiving excellent training in survival and rescue operations. I can speak from experience in this regard, because I believe I am the only member of parliament who has undertaken the army rescue course at the civil defence college at Arnprior. I suggest that such personnel who are trained and disciplined, but not carrying arms of any kind, would be able to demonstrate, particularly to those countries which are still in the process of development and which by coincidence happen to lie in zones subject to earthquakes and floods, that Canada is equally concerned with extending aid to those less fortunate and that our armed forces are capable of exercising themselves for a peaceful purpose.
As a matter of fact, I see that the Canadian army in its recruiting advertisements published in the newspapers claims that the

Canadian soldier is a soldier who works for peace. Another example of the useful role in which our armed forces can be used in peacetime was demonstrated recently when the minister authorized the use of R.C.A.F. aircraft to assist in fighting forest fires in British Columbia. I am sure hon. members will agree that some of the forest fires which we have had can properly be classed as national disasters, in terms of financial loss if not in terms of loss of life. It appears to me, Mr. Chairman, that there will always be a need to meet not only military emergencies but other major disasters springing from natural causes.
In recent years we have Seen more and more nations apply for membership in the United Nations. Some of these nations are the very ones which require the services of a United Nations security force, but the United Nations has not yet been able to create a permanent United Nations security force. Some nations oppose the creation of this permanent security force because they fear that their sovereignty will be infringed upon if the security force is sent into their country by the United Nations. On the other hand, if the Canadian government were to offer to the United Nations a Canadian task force clearly earmarked to meet national emergencies and disasters of other than a military nature, and if this task force were given the opportunity to demonstrate its usefulness, it may very well be that in time a military security force could be formed; because those nations which now have reservations about the creation of a security force would have had demonstrated to them that the United Nations can, in its wisdom, dispatch forces which are not purely of military substance or purpose.
It might be said that there is no need for the creation of such a task force to meet national and international disasters because we have organizations like the international Red Cross. My answer would be that only governments can implement the kind of suggestion I have put forward. Only governments can move quickly in time of great emergency; only nations belong to the United Nations and these nations speak through their elected representatives. The international Red Cross, comprehensive though this organization might be, does not have facilities comparable to those which are available to governments, and that is why I suggest that the Canadian government take my suggestion under consideration.
There is a need to build up, particularly in the newly independent nations, a feeling of trust and confidence in the United Nations. So far the major military powers have dominated the United Nations security council because military situations have taken most

Mr. Chairman, I can do no better than quote Air Vice Marshal Thomas C. Traill of Britain, former central Atlantic NATO air commander who, in speaking to officers and staff at NATO headquarters in March, 1958 said:
The war of arms, if it comes, is an extension of the ideological war. At the higher levels military and ideological strategy are one. Together they form the strategy of this world conflict. If we wish to survive it is madness to consider one in isolation from the other. The enemy is very clear on this. He is equally prepared to take an ideological or a military initiative, to use an ideological or a military weapon. You in this headquarters and the forces you control are here to prevent the enemy attempting to take a short cut to his ideological objective, to prevent him from trying to force his idea on his neighbours with bayonets. The armed forces hold the ring while the war of ideas is fought out. It is essential for our existence that you should hold the ring. But you cannot keep an idea the other side of a frontier with bayonets. You can only do that by taking the offensive with a better and stronger idea. Admiral Radford put it in a nutshell while he was chairman of the United States chiefs of staff. He said, "The military power of the United States and her allies can only buy time".


Canada is under serious, vicious and incessant attack from forces that covet our land and our natural resources and have a determined will to destroy our way of life and freedom. It is therefore obvious that the ideological offensive which Canada must now take and the ideological defences which Canada must now prepare cannot be confined alone to the padre's hour and current events classes, nor to what is vaguely referred to as psychological warfare.

It is possible that we may never have an atomic war. Perhaps we shall never have a conventional war. But we are in danger of living in a continuing subversive war.
