There are others, but these are the most blatant issues. The fact is that through skilfully playing on every kind of motive and human emotion, idealism, love of peace, sentimentality, naivete; sensation loving, vanity and mammon, the Kremlin spokesmen in Canada have been able to seduce thousands of otherwise loyal Canadians and use them for their own purposes.
An interesting example of ideological strategy within our own borders developed from the publication of an editorial in the Vancouver Sun on March 17, 1960. Headed "Self-Satisfied and Dead", the editorial read as follows:
Communism has an ideology, put succinctly in one line of the Red Flag, the communist anthem: "The universal soviet shall be the human race". And it has a purpose, put even more succinctly by Nikita Khrushchev: "We shall bury you".
Has the western world's free society an equally emphatic ideology, an equally clear purpose with which to answer?
That is the question posed by a slim booklec entitled "Ideology and Co-Existence" distributed by Moral Re-Armament to every household in Canada.
The question is not abstract. Call the present state of the world cold war, call it competitive co-existence. The fact remains that it is a struggle. A new kind of struggle-not through armies for territory but through men's minds for world domination.
And in battles of the mind, just as much as in battles of military conquest, victory goes to the strong, the sure and the determined.
Among the booklet's many quotations from world leaders is this, from Chancellor Adenauer of West Germany: "A nation without an ideology is selfsatisfied and dead". Could that be us?
Within the pages of the same Vancouver Sun shortly thereafter appeared a signed column by one of its writers- Using the Hitlerian technique of the big lie he blasted Moral Re-Armament. Within days his article was reproduced in mimeograph form and distributed by the mine, mill and smelter workers union to their members in Trail,

British Columbia, which is in the riding of the member for Kootenay West. Barely four weeks ago a letter from the president of what the member for Kootenay West called "a Trail smelter workers' union" was quoted as evidence for an attack on Moral Re-Armament in this very house. The member failed to mention that this so-called smelter workers' union is in fact the same international union of mine, mill and smelter workers which was kicked out of the Canadian Labour Congress for being communist dominated, and is widely known as being run on its national level by Moscow-trained men.
It is little wonder that another source drawn on in the same speech in this house was that well known pacifist, Rev. Donald Soper, who bluntly announced over the C.B.C. television network a few weeks ago "Khrushchev is our man". This is also the same C.B.C. whose officials a short while ago denied in writing the opportunity for time to be made available, or even paid for, so that Canadians might hear of a moral ideology and an effective answer to the Khrushchev whom Dr. Soper so ardently admires. This is a striking instance of the extent to which the subversive strategy to thwart freedom of speech has already advanced on an issue of vital national importance. It is an example of the ideological war already being waged inside our own borders. The fact is that any force which exposes subversive strategy and tactics and clarifies the true moral basis for democracy in terms of a superior ideology is bound to come under attack. It has been a source of great hope and encouragement for those who see the subversive strategy in Canada today to know there is a forceful and effective positive strategy at work.
The handbook "Ideology and Co-Existence" was distributed to each of the 4,340,000 homes in Canada in early March. The response was nation-wide, and revealed the extent of understanding and sense of need for positive ideological initiative in this country. One in four of all the daily newspapers in Canada wrote forthright editorials welcoming the distribution. Literally hundreds of Canadians wrote letters of thanks for the booklet and asked for further information. "Ideology and Co-Existence" impacted every field of national life, politics, labour, industry, church, women's work, education and farm organizations. I quote from a feature article in the Hamilton Spectator of April 14:
The battle line is being drawn in Canada. Canadians are being faced with the basic issues in the war of ideas more sharply than ever before.
This article reports fully on the background of Moral Re-Armament, how and why it

has been attacked by fascists and communists alike. It tells of the sacrificial financial contributions of hundreds of people, and continues:

The Edmonton Journal, in an editorial on March 7, called the distribution of "Ideology and Co-Existence" a major contribution to the democratic cause in the cold war's ideological struggle. The Regina Leader-Post wrote:
This is a tremendous, timely and creative project. It is one that must be and will be welcomed by every free man and woman who knows the measure and purpose of the communist threat- and, in the same breath, is uncomfortably aware of that western lack of purpose and focus that is presently of major concern to alert western leaders.

-clarifies the basic issues facing the free nations of the world and shows how they can take initiative in the east-west ideological war. The aim of the booklet is to strengthen the backbone of freedom and instil the will to fight for what is right.
The Windsor Star wrote:
Military strength is necessary but it is dangerous to rely on it entirely. If the struggle against the communist ideology is to be won, it must be won in the hearts and minds of men.

The manifesto "Ideology and Co-Existence" which will be sent out to every Canadian home expresses in clear terms the true ideology of the free world and offers an answer to communism.
These are but a few of the editorials published on this subject. They and the hundreds of letters have revealed that there is a great body of support in this country for clear ideological initiative and action. I should like here and now, Mr. Chairman, to pay tribute to a great friend of Canada, to a man whom a British diplomat has evaluated in the following words:
He saw the significance of this underlying ideological struggle years ahead of most other public figures, and his published speeches over the past 20 and 25 years prove it. But he did not stop there. He did a second thing.
He faced the consquences of this ideological struggle and began to think out what democracy's answering, positive ideology was. And then he did a third thing. He built a world force of people, ideologically equipped and living out the answer in their own lives.
I refer to Dr. Frank N. D. Buchman, Pennsylvania-born initiator of the program of Moral Re-Armament. Dr. Buchman came to this country in 1932. He was a friend of the then prime minister, the late R. B. Bennett. Mr. Bennett told Dr. Buchman at that time:

Speaking as a statesman I am convinced that the influences which you so powerfully represent are the only ones which can save the world today.

I repeat that the ideological initiative which Canada must now take and the ideological defence that Canada must now prepare cannot be confined alone to the padre's hour and current events classes for soldiers, nor to what is vaguely referred to as psychological warfare. This issue of national purpose is fundamental in relation to the question of national defence. More and more is being written on this subject. Few who write have had the insight and courage to give this term meaning for the individual citizen. National purpose must mean that we as a nation know what we are living for. To have a strong national purpose a nation's citizens must be able to answer in positive terms the simple question, "What am I living for?" A collective national will must be the collected individual wills of Canadians, the will to know what they stand for, to love what they know and to be ready to fight for what they love. A rather ingenious method is used which gives students at that college an opportunity to learn both languages. The method is as follows: for a certain period of time, say two or three weeks, all courses are given in English, and English conversation is the rule; then in the next period it is the opposite, and all conversations in the college must be carried on in French, so that by the time they leave the college, on completion of their courses, the students are fully bilingual, which, of course is a decided asset to them, and one which is looked for by so many Canadian employers.

I said no such thing, Mr. Chairman. What I said was that if the issues were purely political or psychological we would have nothing to fear.

speechtext: Order. The hon. member for Kootenay West must of course accept the statement of the hon. member.

Yes, Mr. Chairman, I have, but I wanted to explain on what basis I made my statement. Now we are getting along beautifully.
If the government understood the facts of life in the nuclear age we would not hear such nonsense from the minister as his description-at the top of page 7526 of Hansard -of the third role given the army, namely: -to maintain a force capable of taking action against any possible commando-type raid in the Arctic or elsewhere in Canada.
I know that this particular type of madness was first dreamt up by the Liberals back in 1946 so that a role could be found for the army brigade of those days. The idea that the 79951-0-4821
Supply-National Defence Russians would risk an almost certain thermonuclear response from SAC for the sake of effecting a small lodgement on the North American continent is nothing short of preposterous. What we have here is an attempt to fashion a potential aggressor's action to our own capabilities instead of doing the only sensible thing which is to calculate what a potential aggressor is likely to do and then figure out what we can do about it.
Our aim must be to prevent war for a thermonuclear war would be suicide. If the government really understood this we would not have had before us in recent days the spectacle of the government buying four Caribou aircraft so we could carry out our United Nations commitment in the Congo. I should like to ask the minister to reply on this point at the appropriate time.
Our armed forces, despite their impressive strength of 122,000 all ranks, are totally inadequate to carry out operations under the United Nations, yet it is precisely for such operations that the bulk of our armed forces should be organized. I say this because it is the efficient and prompt carrying out of United Nations operations that will prevent small wars and incidents from developing into a thermonuclear catastrophe.
We say that what we need are the complete unification of our armed forces and the development of all-arms teams capable of rapid transportation anywhere in the world for operation under the United Nations, ranging from a convention war on the Korean model to actions similar to those on the borders of Israel and in the Congo. For this purpose and for the purpose of deterring thermonuclear attack on Canada we do not need submarines, which the government seems to be advocating, nor do we need inter-cepters in Canada which the Liberals advocate and toward the provision of which the government appears to be moving, nor do we need the new destroyer-escorts which the government is building.
Further proof, if proof were needed, of the government's inability to understand the difference between defence and the deterrent is to be found at page 7556 of Hansard for August 4. Talking about nuclear warheads for Bomarcs the minister had this to say:
To declare in advance that we would never use such weapons would weaken immeasurably their deterrent effect. Do not let us overlook the importance of the deterrent. I emphasized that many times during the course of this speech. Thus, if we announce that we are not going to use them we would be decreasing our ability to prevent war, which is the main object of all our defence preparations. Such a declaration would give a would-be aggressor great comfort and would facilitate the preparations of his plans, as he would know the limitations of our defence.

Supply-National Defence
That is what the hon. gentleman said, and I have read his remarks over very carefully. What the government fails to understand, from our point of view, is this: Deterrence lies in the power to attack, to retaliate. It does not lie in the power to defend, since it is not possible to develop a defence against weapons having the power of 20 million tons of T.N.T.
That is the major thesis that I wish to put forward in connection with this defence problem on behalf of the members of this group. I wish to bring to the attention of the government the changing attitude of the people of this country toward these matters and I am sure that the change in the attitude of the Liberal party has come about as a result of a recognition of a change in the climate of opinion in Canada during the last 12 months with respect to defence. I give them credit for responding to this change in public opinion and for announcing a policy 12 months after the C.C.F. had taken precisely that same stand in the House of Commons.
But I must stop proceeding along those lines, because I see the hon. member for Trinity glaring at me again. It does not look pretty when he glares. He has a happy nature on most occasions and it is not in character for him to glare. I suppose he is annoyed at something, and I presume something the minister has said has caused his annoyance.
I have received a good deal of correspondence in connection with this subject, as no doubt, have most other hon. members of this house, much of which illustrates my contention that public opinion with respect to nuclear warfare is changing. I have in my hand a letter from some faculty members of McMaster University which indicates that they have given serious study to this question. It is an open letter which was sent to the Canadian government, and no doubt the minister as well as other hon. members have received copies. I do not intend to read it. They deal fully with the reasons for composing the letter, and then emphasize six points with respect to the general disarmament negotiations. Point No. 5 reads as follows:
Canada should not acquire nuclear weapons under any system of control and should oppose the arming of NATO with such weapons.
Then they say in Point No. 6:
Canada should seek the adoption by NATO of a policy of neutralization of central Europe-
That, as hon. members will recognize, is the policy of the C.C.F. party.
-and should support any step in that direction.
We are not concerned with emphasizing that that is C.C.F. policy. We are only too glad to see increasing numbers of persons

and responsible groups in Canada expressing the same opinions that have been expressed by members of this group.
I come, now, to a short article which appeared in the Torch, a magazine published for ex-service men and women. The Torch is a magazine of a well-known veterans' organization in this country, and in the issue of November, 1959 appeared an article on defence entitled "The Past, the Present, the Future" by Mr. E. V. (Gene) Heesaker, the Ontario provincial president of the Canadian Corps Association. I am sure hon. gentlemen facing me are not going to question this man's loyalty to Canada or suggest he belongs to a subversive group. This man has a war record of which he can be proud. Here is what he had to say on page 15 of this magazine:
The questions now to be decided are: shall we continue to pour money into weapons that will not protect us? Or shall we divert that money to building and healing, which humanity desperately needs? Shall we join the nuclear arms race-a race to the death? Or shall we declare ourselves out of it? I believe Canada should stop buying weapons that can't give us security in this nuclear age. We should cut our so-called defence spending sharply and put that money to better use for human well-being.
Economically, Canada can contribute to the fight against communism and reap 20 times the value for every dollar now spent on weapons, provided we get out of an arms race which we cannot afford. This would not mean lower taxes and more pleasure spending, but that we would divert the money from bombers into food and technical assistance for the hungry millions of Asia and Africa. Our most shattering defeat would be the collapse of Nehru's India and its swing to communism along with China. In my way of thinking, the greatest bulwark against world communism would be India's success in emerging from colonialism into democracy and becoming an example for Asia and Africa.
This change of direction is not going to be easy for us. It will require dynamiting of our mental log jam on the whole problem of the communist threat to our western democracy.
I suggest that if we take that veteran's views and the views of others which have been presented in similar terms we would get much further along on the road to peace than we shall by circulating the pamphlet "Co-existence" to the armed forces and conducting courses in ideological warfare. I have a letter here from Mrs. Josephine Davis of the central committee of the Voice of Women expressing similar views. She says:
At a large representative inaugural meeting Voice of Women unanimously declared itself opposed to nuclear war. Therefore we support any proposal which will keep Canada free from nuclear armament, thereby strengthening Canada's leadership among non-nuclear powers.
I might mention that these ladies visited the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition and the leader of this group, and all the leaders of the parties in this house

wished them well with their crusade. The Prime Minister is reported as having said: Carry on, ladies; you are doing good work; we recognize your sincerity, and so on. And the Prime Minister was quite correct in saying that.
I want to finish up by saying that we fully appreciate the task which the Minister of National Defence has before him. We are living under changing conditions and I do not underestimate the problems which are bound to face any minister of defence in these days. If I might supplement the views put forward yesterday by the hon. member for Vancouver East, we believe our forces should be provided with aircraft capable of transporting them to any part of the world where the United Nations might need their assistance, such as the Congo where an emergency exists at the present time. We are glad that parliament endorsed the action which the government took with regard to the Congo situation, and we have been proved correct in our point of view about that situation. We said just a few days ago that the United Nations should take action and go into Katanga and that is the course which is apparently being followed. But to take action of that kind requires, of course, the necessary forces. Once again the C.C.F. approach to the question has been proved correct in less than a week by the march of events.
I am nearly finished but I do not know what time I have left since I have been interrupted by the hon. member for Trinity.
This matter has been a source of concern to the Belgian socialists. I have here a copy of a statement made by Mr. Victor Larock, M.P., executive member of the Belgian socialist party and former foreign minister of Belgium. What does he say? I mention this to indicate the need for our being ready and armed and having forces to support the United Nations activity. This statement was made on June 20:
History will record that in the hour of withdrawal the administration, big business and its press in the Congo have at least maintained one tenacious sentiment: anti-socialism.
However, when the fate of 13 million human beings is at the mercy of improvised decisions, the most legitimate of political grievances must be silent.
Two dangers are threatening the Congo: that of tribal struggles which can from one day to the next become murderous again, and that of the separatisms which would inevitably lead to the disintegration of the country.
"What do we care? They wanted to be free; their fate no longer concerns us!" There is cowardice in such language. It is the language of the investor which has rid himself of his stocks and shares. Belgium did not grant independence to the most beautiful and richest of territories in Africa in order to surrender it to civil war, dismemberment and the greed of foreigners.
Supply-National Defence
Then, he goes on to advocate strong action by the United Nations. I mention this to illustrate the need for a United Nations force which is ready to go into action. We are proud that Canada is participating in that force at the present time. From our point of view we urge that we should be ready to participate at any time and our forces should be trained on that basis.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, on behalf of this group, I wish to say that we recognize the devotion to duty of all ranks and all that is being done by the various sections of the Canadian armed forces, the navy the army and the air force. Hon. members will be surprised at how interested our men in the armed forces are in defence policy and in international affairs. I judge that from the correspondence we get from them. You know, Mr. Chairman, I have boys who write me from the Arctic and ask me to ask the minister this or that question. That is all to the good; that is democracy and it shows that our armed forces are interested in this problem.
I do urge that the minister and the government give consideration to these proposals which are the result of study and thought by members of this group who place them before the committee in all sincerity, believing they are to the best advantage of this Canada which we all love.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Kootenay West and my breakfast partner has been particularly provocative this afternoon, which is not his usual attitude, I must say. As he indicated to the committee, he served his country in world war I with distinction and for that we honour him.
Since that, too.

Unfortunately, as he said, he was wounded a number of times in battle and this reminds me of a story which he has told me at breakfast at least two or three times. I would not be presumptuous enough to mention it if he himself did not say it about himself, namely that on returning home his father, referring to what had happened to him, said that he was aware that this was indeed unfortunate but that it had affected the judgment of the hon. gentleman and that he has not been exactly the same since.
That was a reference to the Liberal party.

My father was somewhat prejudiced, Mr. Chairman.
7632	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence
If there is any correction I should be glad to yield so that the hon. gentleman may put it on the record.
My father was a very fine old gentleman, but he had all the prejudices that the Liberals have on political occasions.

However, Mr. Chairman, for the next few minutes I think what I am going to say will be approved of by the hon. member for Kootenay West, and I hope it will commend itself to the Minister of National Defence. I should like to deal specifically for a few minutes, if I may, with the matter of North American air defence. I mentioned this in my statement yesterday and the minister mentioned it in his rebuttal both before and after I had spoken.
I say that the government's policy on air defence is inconsistent and unrealistic. The recommendations of the special select committee on defence expenditures indicated that the bomber threat is diminishing. This view is subscribed to by the government and, indeed, was put on the record by the Prime Minister and the Minister of National Defence both at the time the Avro Arrow interceptor was cancelled. Now on the basis of the information available, and on the basis of a study of the minister's statements we have come to the conclusion that the bomber threat will be of real significance in proportion to the total threat against the North American continent for a very short period of time, perhaps another two or three years.
From that time on, Mr. Chairman, the overwhelming threat will be from missiles, particularly the intercontinental ballistic missiles. Once that has happened, unless there is some scientific breakthrough, as yet not contemplated by western scientists, there will be no effective air defence of the North American continent. Yet the minister in his statement kept referring to the deterrent. He returned to this a number of times and spoke about Canada's contribution to the deterrent. The presumption was that at least the installation of the SAGE-Bomarc system was a contribution to the western, and more particularly the United States, deterrent.
That is what the North American air defence was set up for. We used to be completely honest and admit that the air defence of the North American continent was designed to protect the retaliatory capacity of the strategic air command; it was never really intended to do anything else. When the proposal for the Bomarc sites first arrived there was no discussion of the defence of Canada per se, but only a consideration in terms of defence of the retaliatory capacity of the west and of the strategic air command. Only in


the last year or two has there been creeping into statements on this subject some reference to the possible defence of Canadian cities and civilian population as a result of this defensive arrangement. Now, however, time has overtaken the Bomarc-SAGE system.
I should like to put on the record some supporting evidence in this respect. I should like to quote first of all from an article by Brigadier General Thomas R. Phillips, United States army, retired, as quoted in evidence in hearings before the subcommittee of the committee on appropriations of the United States senate. General Phillips had this to say in reference to the Bomarc:
Time has overtaken it. The idea was broached in 1948. First study contracts were let in 1950 to Boeing Airplane Company and the University of Michigan for research and design studies.
It was designed to cope with the subsonic aircraft anticipated to be in service in 1954 or 1955.
Our objection to the Bomarc from the standpoint of defence in that period from the mid-60's forward has been on the basis that it is a fixed installation. We put clearly on the record that it was not its failures which alarmed us, although this was an additional matter of concern, but the fact that time had overtaken the whole SAGE-Bomarc system and that fixed installations in the time period for which it will be in operation will render it too vulnerable to be effective.
I should like to quote a few witnesses in respect of the matter of fixed installations or fixed bases. The first one I should like to quote is the United States secretary of defence, Mr. Gates. In evidence before the subcommittee of the committee on appropriations of the house of representatives, referring to the SAGE-Bomarc system he said:
-I mean In the course of fiscal year 1961, that we have another re-appraisal. Such a re-appraisal might change the emphasis on certain factors, in which case there might be a change in the air defence plan. I know there have been some further studies on the air defence problem, not along the lines of the F-108 but along the line of reconsidering the continued use, in numbers, of aircraft interceptors. One of the reasons for this is that the Bomarc sites themselves are vulnerable, as fixed sites, to good, accurate missiles.
No one has denied that the soviet imperialists have good, accurate missiles. Then, the Right Hon. Harold Watkinson indicated at the time of the cancellation of the Blue Streak that the primary reason for the cancellation of that weapons system was because it would be fired from fixed bases and as such would be too vulnerable on the ground to enemy missilry. Assuming that the Russians would in the case of an all-out war strike first, any fixed installation, offensive or defensive, is vulnerable to attack by missile.
Would the hon. member permit a question?
Certainly.

Is the hon. member for Trinity aware that the minister of national defence of Great Britain explained quite clearly during his recent visit to Canada that although the so-called fixed sites which would have been used for the Blue Streak missile in England could be vulnerable Canada was far enough away so that the same dangers do not apply here as applied in Great Britain?

Mr. Chairman, I had a very pleasant chat with the right hon. gentleman, thanks to the good offices of the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of National Defence, and there was no doubt from talking to him that as a matter of principle he believes that fixed installations in the years that lie ahead are too vulnerable to missilry. However, I am sure he would be diplomatic enough not to comment on those specific matters coming within the competence of the Canadian government. This view was supported by his chief scientific adviser, Sir Solly Zucterman, who was of exactly the same opinion that fixed bases, either offensive or defensive, from the mid-60's on were so vulnerable as to make their use virtually untenable.
Field Marshal Viscount Montgomery has taken the same position and has spoken very strongly against any future plans for the installation of fixed bases, again on the basis of their vulnerability. General Phillips, again referring specifically to the Bomarc, said this:
Bomarc suffers from three main difficulties that have overtaken it with time: (1) It has proved impossible to make it effective against supersonic targets; (2) it has been so long in development the bombers can now fly as fast as the interceptor; and (3) it is a sitting duck on its large bases, with 60 missiles on each, for attack by enemy ballistic missiles.
Then, General White, chief of staff of the United States air force, had this to say in evidence before the senate subcommittee:
I will say this: If we developed the Skyboat to conclusion and if the soviets do a similar one with a thousand mile range, obviously the Bomarc is not going to be an adequate defence against that type of weapon.
He goes on to say that this would not be true in the immediate future, presumably referring to the next two or three years. Again, General White in giving evidence before the same senate committee was asked a question by Senator Symington, who was referring to General Phillips' article, and I read the following passage:
Senator Symington: General Phillips' third point is that: "It (Bomarc) is a sitting duck on its large bases, with 60 missiles on each, for attack by enemy ballistic missiles." How about that?
General White: I think that is true. It is vulnerable, yes, sir.
