Mr. Chairman, there are only two supporters of Bomarc, the Canadian government and NORAD, not the people of Canada. We can understand the government's dilemma. It is one of its own making. In our opinion it might just as well get out of that dilemma now before congress embarrasses it again. I am convinced that congress would not have reinstated-
Are they going to have another election next year?
Is the hon. member implying that the reason for the reinstatement of the Bomarc program this year is that they are having a presidential election?
No.
That was the inference I took from his statement.
Cuts were made.

On the contrary, the hon. member has been in politics long enough to know that you do not cut a work-making program just in advance of a general election. I think that is what the hon. member had in mind, before he had time to reflect on it.
Just the contrary.

I am convinced that congress would not have reinstated the Bomarc except for Mr. Khrushchev and his boorish behaviour at the summit conference and the pressure of their feeling for the Canadian government. They may, of course, have a change of heart again in the future. They certainly will if they take a cold look at the whole situation.
With respect to NORAD, I had the privilege of visiting NORAD headquarters this year and I was considerably disturbed by what I saw there. NORAD is living in a dream world four to five years behind the times. From here on in they are going to suffer from one of the seemingly inevitable laws of both military and government service, Parkinson's law. They are going to have to keep busy whether or not their function remains as useful as it has been in the past. By the mid-60's the effectiveness of NORAD to protect the deterrent will be reduced to something inconsequential. They cannot possibly stop intercontinental ballistic missiles, and under questioning they will admit this but only reluctantly. It is a difficult thing to accept that there is not at the present time and there is no prospect in the immediate future of an adequate defence against the intercontinental ballistic missile.

Why did you vote against my motion?

Supply-National Defence

Yet they have the responsibility for so-called air defence of the North American continent. Their position is natural but their evidence must be considered on the basis of the bias and self-interest it inevitably contains. An indication of the United States defence department's appraisal of the future of NORAD is contained in the fact that there were some plans to harden the NORAD headquarters. A hole was being cut out of the Colorado mountains for this purpose. This project was cancelled. If the United States defence department had rated NORAD's future functions as indispensable, the project would not have been cancelled. NORAD headquarters is soft and vulnerable. By the mid-1960's its continuing effective function will be primarily the detection and identification roles.
If there were an all-out war, if missiles were used at the outset as would likely be the case, in that time period NORAD headquarters itself would likely be an early target. This, of course, would be proof positive that an all-out offensive had commenced. Unfortunately it would be a little late if there were no warning before that.
This brings up the whole question of timing. When will the whole SAGE-Bomarc system be in operation? What does United States Secretary Gates say about it?
I should like to know what you say about it. You have changed your mind in the last two hours.
I have not changed my stand. If you check the record you will find out. Secretary Gates, before the house committee on appropriations, had this to say in reply to a question from Mr. Minshall:

When will the program be completely finished?
Secretary Gates: Completely in being?

Completely in being.
Secretary Gates: By the end of fiscal year 1963.
Well, Mr. Chairman, 1963 is too late. The Canadian government is spending the taxpayers' money on a system which will be too late to be useful enough to justify the expenditure.
May I ask the hon. member a question? What does he mean by "too late"? Is he referring to NORAD?

I am referring to the SAGE-Bomarc system. After that, the only continuing useful role, as I said, will be detection and identification to prevent bombers sneaking in and being well on their way before the ICBM's are fired. Our suggestion that we have a few interceptors for the identification role seems to us to make sense. It gives us some element of sovereignty over Canadian air space and provides a useful

service to the United States deterrent. The government's present Bomarc program will be useless to prevent war and equally useless in case an all-out war should break out.
The minister in this respect, has been inconsistent. He told us in the committee on defence expenditures that the Bomarc is not a substitute for the manned interceptor, that it is complementary to it. However, a decision has been made by the government to go ahead and build a SAGE-Bomarc system which will not be, according to what Secretary Gates says, completely in operation until 1963, and yet at the same time, to be inconsistent, has not made a decision to replace the Canadian air defence squadrons. If the minister really believes that there is any such thing as air defence after the mid-1960's, he should have made a decision in respect of the air defence squadrons long ago.
Actually I suppose I should not point the finger too much in the direction of the Minister of National Defence because I think he has at least a view in connection with this matter. I believe this particular egg is in the Prime Minister's nest at the present time, and he is waiting to see what will be hatched from it. The minister has told us that the matter is under continuing consideration. He also told us that no quick decision should be made. Surely, you could not accuse the minister of making a quick decision on a matter which has been under consideration for at least a year and a half. If that is what this government calls quick, I should like to see what they call mature consideration. They call this continuing consideration, and that applies to most of the projects on which they have to make a decision.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I should like the minister to tell this committee if, in his opinion, after the mid-1960's the contribution to the deterrent of the two Bomarc squadrons will be of any real significance. Will he answer me as to those objections that have been raised in respect of their vulnerability and uselessness in this time period? This is a serious thing. It is difficult, I know, for the minister to realize that by the time he gets this system into operation it will be obsolete and out of date. I should like his assurance that he has considered the matter fully, and I should like him to tell the committee if, in his considered judgment, he is satisfied that its usefulness, from the mid-1960's on, will be sufficient to justify the expenditure of one cent of the Canadian taxpayers' money.

I do not intend to speak more than one minute. I just have to express my admiration for the absolute consistency of the inconsistency of the hon. member for

Trinity. It was only about two hours ago that he had an opportunity of showing whether he thought the expenditure on NORAD should be continued, and he said yes. During the last five minutes he has been giving every reason he possibly could as to why NORAD is useless, inefficient and hopeless. I say I admire the consistency of his inconsistency. I am very proud of the fact that at least we have the courage of our convictions at all times.
I shall have to answer that short interjection which was put on the record.

Of course, the inspiration
always comes from this group.
The hon. gentleman seems to be incapable of differentiation. If he had listened to this speech of mine yesterday, which he said he had read before it was delivered-
And heard it, too.

-he would have determined that whereas we take the position the SAGE-Bomarc program is not worth continuing because by the time it is installed it will be too late, we do say there is a continuing requirement for detection and identification. This requirement will continue to be essential for a number of years so the strategic air command, or whatever the unit in charge of the retaliatory power of the western world is called can be informed if there should be Russian bombers over Canadian air territory. You have to have some equipment to do that. We have also said that under the present agreement there are certain advantages in liaison which reduces the reaction time, and so on.
For that reason we have said that we could not go back on the agreement unless it could be proved that those functions could be carried out just as effectively outside; that has not been proved to our satisfaction. Surely the hon. gentleman can see the difference between those two points of view.

May I just add one word? I feel it is now time that this house came to a close, out of consideration for the C.C.F., because if it continues much longer the Liberals will have stolen many more of our policies.

Mr. Chairman, as you know I had the privilege of serving on the special committee on defence expenditures. Surely that was not on account of my competency in the field of defence; it was only because I was also privileged last year and this year
Supply-National Defence to serve on the Canada-United States parliamentary group and to serve on the special subcommittee on defence and disarmament of that group.
I was very sorry that I had to miss some of the meetings of the committee, because of some personal unavoidable circumstances, but when I was absent I was very ably replaced, I am sure, by my hon. colleague from Rich elieu-V er cher es.
I just want to make a few brief remarks with respect to this first item. I do not want to go back on what was said by my leader and by my friend from Trinity as to how this committee was formed, as to when it was formed or as to how it functioned. The remarks I want to make relate especially to the army. It is my opinion that as it is now the army has not enough mobility. You know, Mr. Chairman, that in world war I it was a war almost of immobility. In world war II it became a mobile war after the German army moved very quickly through all the lands of Europe.
In the years to come there is no doubt that the army has to be, as I would say, super-mobile, and every device should be considered to make it mobile to the fullest extent. I think the army should be capable of being airlifted through its own airlift operations if possible; if not, through close coordination with the R.C.A.F. Also, troopships should be available at all times. If this is not possible on account of financial limitations, pre-arrangements should be made with commercial boat lines so that in the event of war on the continent of Europe reinforcements could be provided very quickly to our brigade group over there.
The next thing I want to speak of is national survival. That has to do, especially in Canada, with the army. Perhaps I may read the statement of the Minister of National Defence which was given to the special committee on defence expenditures. I am reading from the pamphlet that was distributed, which is entitled, "Information for the special committee on defence expenditures 1960". This pamphlet is dated May, 1960 and paragraph 15 reads:
15.	Duties and responsibilities assigned to the army in survival operations became effective on September 1, 1959, On that date the national survival attack warning system commenced operations on a permanent 24-hour a day basis. Orders have already been placed for light rescue equipment and radiac instruments for the mobile units and sufficient quantities for training have now been delivered. By the end of 1960 most radiac and rescue items will be available to meet both training and operational requirements.
The next paragraph, No. 16, says:
16.	The militia has been issued with sufficient equipment to start training in survival operations.

Supply-National Defence Additional rescue equipment will be provided this year in order that the reserve units can perform their full survival role.
It has been said that the strength of the regular army as of May of this year was 47,185, and the strength of the militia was 40,010. The role of national survival, of course, is specially related to the public in general. I read this in the Journal of the Stanford Research Institute, fourth quarter, 1959, volume 3, in an article by Mr. Rogers Cannell. I cite from page 182 at the top of the page:
People have been led to believe that one nuclear weapon could destroy an entire city, so they conclude that no type of protection can be effective. Preoccupation with this notion has obscured the truth: protective actions can be quite effective not only at distances from a target city but also within it.
Starting from that statement I think that in the United States as well as in Canada people do not appreciate the danger that may lie from an all-out nuclear attack. We all hope, of course, that there will be no such attack in our time or for very many years to come. But if it should come, people should know what to do.
We have also been told that one part of the task of the regular army is its operation with regard to national survival. I have read from the record that the regular army will be fully equipped this year. That does not mean that the regular army will be fully trained. I hope, and I suppose that the government's policy in this regard is that by early next year the regular army will be completely trained for that kind of operation. But the regular army has no direct and regular dealing with the majority of the people of this country. On that I think we should rest our case.
In my home town there is a militia unit of engineers. I know that they have started to train for survival operations. I also know that they are not fully equipped. I hope and urge the government to see that this reserve unit, like all other units in Canada, is fully equipped as soon as possible, and also that the militia will be fully trained in that regard.
It is my thinking that the regular army should be in constant touch with the militia and that experts in that field should be attached to militia units, to train them for survival operations. In turn, the public at large should, I think, be invited, when the militia is fully trained, to attend those training exercises so that the people will know what to do and what to expect in case of emergency.
More than that, the people of this country should be urged and asked to take part in those rescue operations and to take part in that training so that if it happens that there is an emergency, there will be no panic or


anything of that sort among the people of this country. In that way the civilians of the country will co-operate fully with the militia in their own vicinity, and with the regular army.
In finishing, Mr. Chairman, I do not want to go further because, as I said before, I do not want to go too far. But I do think that every trooper in the militia should be fully trained in signalization and communications in order to establish prompt and constant communication with the general public in the event of an emergency. With this in view the Canadian people will know what to do.
I have one question I would like to put to the minister dealing entirely with another matter, and it is with regard to the Congo situation. I would like to learn from the minister later on if there is a French speaking unit which is to be dispatched to the Congo, because in that part, as we know, most of the people speak in French.

Mr. Chairman, during the course of this discussion both the Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Trinity complained quite often that the members of the special committee had little opportunity to ask or were prevented from asking any question relating to government policy in the defence of Canada.
I can assure you, Mr. Chairman, and hon. members of the House of Commons that they were certainly given every opportunity to examine our defence program. A good deal of latitude, far more than in previous defence committees, was given to the members of the committee in asking questions. Anyone who doubts this need only read the committee reports.
There were 26 meetings of the committee and the minister was given adequate time to explain our defence policy and the steps we were taking to carry out defence commitments, and all the members without exception, except when irresponsible statements were made and sometimes foolish questions asked, were given every opportunity to carry on their interrogation of the minister.
I would just like to give a rundown of some of the comments by the minister in answer to the criticism of the Leader of the Opposition. On June 1 the minister made a statement to the committee regarding the general defence policy and also in relation to the United Nations. On June 3 the minister made a statement regarding our participation in NATO; and on June 8, our participation in NORAD.
On June 10 the minister made some detailed remarks concerning national survival, and then the chairman allowed questions on all of these matters. Certainly they were not

debates, but I must say that a great many of these questions were prefaced by some very long statements. All these statements made by the minister were incorporated into a booklet of 37 pages entitled "Canadian defence policy", and this booklet is available to all members of the House of Commons. Perhaps they will now peruse this book and I hope the Leader of the Opposition looks at it as well and takes some cognizance of some of the statements made by the minister in answers to questions.
In order to substantiate these remarks I would like to cite a few of the questions asked by opposition members to show how much latitude they were given in asking questions about policy and how much information the minister gave in return. At page 372 of the committee report the hon. member for Trinity asked this question:
I would like the minister to explain, again, in greater detail why, when the Bomarc is supposed to be an area defence, following the long-range manned interceptors, it has not been the announced policy of the Canadian government to follow that plan.
In answer to this question the minister said:
I do not know that you can define the Bomarc and the interceptors as being a first line and a second line of defence. There are two elements in the defence of the North American continent against the bomber attack, interceptors and the ground-to-air missile; and those are integrated across the continent. Some of those elements are provided by Canada, and some of those elements are provided by the United States.
Perhaps this did not satisfy the hon. member for Trinity because on page 374 he asked this question:
-why did not the minister recommend that the funds of both the United States and Canada, which are to be, he hopes assigned to the Bomarc system, be allocated rather to a strengthening of the offensive and to the making of a more mobile offensive force?
In answer to that the minister said:
Because there has to be a proper balance kept between the two. We have strived to reach that at a reasonable balance, and, as you know, the United States are placing a higher proportion of their available funds into the development of the retaliatory forces.
Then the hon. member for Trinity asked this question:
Does NORAD have plans for weapons which would be of some effect against missiles launched from submarines?
The minister replied:
I have said several times that there is no weapon at present which is capable of destroying a missile which is launched either from a ground launcher, a submarine or an aircraft. The power of defence against those is the fear of retaliation, and retaliation would take place as soon as the missile is launched, whether it is launched from a ground launcher, an aeroplane or a submarine.
Supply-National Defence Then further on page 376 the hon. member for Trinity asked:
Mr. Chairman, it has been stated the main purpose of North American air defence is to defend the deterrent. I wonder if the minister would explain not only what is meant by that but also the mechanics by which it would operate, and what you might anticipate would happen in case of attack?
The chairman did not interfere and the minister did not hesitate at all in his reply. He said:
If there was an attack by bombers, or with the few missiles which the Russians may now have, I would imagine that the main attack, in the first instance, would be directly against the SAC bases, be they bomber bases or missile bases. As soon as the warning was given, I imagine many of the SAC bombers would leave the ground and possibly proceed in the direction of the targets to which they had been assigned. They can always be called back, as you know, once they have started. The defence would come into action against the bombers, hoping to destroy as large a proportion of the bombers as they could. In the meantime, if the Russian bombers continued and started using nuclear weapons, I imagine all the retaliatory forces, wherever they may be, would go into operation against targets in Russia.
These are quite clear statements of policy so far as NORAD and this government are concerned, and I do not know what more the hon. member for Trinity desires. On page 359 of the committee report the hon. member asked:
The suggestion has been put forward by the leader of the Liberal party that NORAD should become an integral part of NATO. What is the minister's feeling in respect of that suggestion?
The minister replied:
NORAD is part of the NATO concept in that it is looking after and providing the defence of the Canadian-United States region of NATO. This is so far removed, at the present time, from the European activities of NATO that I do not think the European members of NATO would have the time to be able to take an intimate interest in the Canadian-United States region. The activities in the development of defences of the Canadian-United States region are explained at the various NATO meetings. There never has been any indication from our European partners that would have any desire to take a part in the defences of this Canadian-United States region. They mainly are interested in the exchange of warning information. NORAD also is interested in obtaining the early warning from the warning systems in Europe. So the main point of contact is the early warning that can be given either to Europe by the Canadian-United States region or to the North American continent by the European system.
The hon. member for Burin-Burgeo asked this question as reported on page 374:
Assuming that hostilities broke out between Russia and the United States and that intercontinental missiles were used on both sides, would it not be necessary to have a follow-up by land troops to consolidate victory? I mean, would it be necessary for each side to follow up with land troops?

Supply-National Defence
To which the minister replied:
Not necessarily. One side or the other might gain such a decisive victory that the government of the other side would feel it desirable to sue for peace. I can foresee such devastating destruction delivered to Russia, if Russia had made the first strike, that the government would collapse and that there would be no necessity to have land armies to occupy Russia. It would be a question of rehabilitating those parts of the world which had been destroyed. That is the second phase of the war. It is pretty hard to predict the actual nature of that, but I certainly do not think that land invasion, as we used to know it, with long military operations, is inevitable.
I was interested this morning when the Leader of the Opposition was making his prolonged speech to note the inconsistencies between what he said and what was said by the official spokesman for the party on defence matters. In the well-publicized speech by the hon. member for Trinity he criticized the purchase of F-104 aircraft for our air force in Europe and argued that we should get an aircraft of a different type which would be of greater use as a low altitude tactical weapon. On the other hand, this morning the Leader of the Opposition said we should not go into this sort of business but we should have high altitude supersonic interceptors.
The Leader of the Opposition endorses the policy I put forward in that respect.

Then I think you should get together in reading each other's speeches or at least have somebody writing those speeches to combine them to some extent so that they might be at least consistent. The Leader of the Opposition said this morning he thought it was very important that our troops should be trained to be airborne so that they could be flown for service anywhere in the world where they might be needed. That is quite different from what was said by the hon. member for Trinity who advised we should have naval craft to carry our troops in assault landing craft instead of aircraft.
They should be able to get anywhere they are going.

There is a little difference in time involved. I should think it would be impossible to have these men trained to be airborne in addition to receiving training in connection with assault craft landings.
Again, this morning the Leader of the Opposition said no time whatever was given to this question of psychological warfare. As a matter of fact I think this subject came up a number of times in the committee. It was brought up by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo, and he brought in a book by one of the leaders of Moral Re-Armament and tried to stuff it down the throats of the committee.
[Mr. Fairfield.l
This was the psychological weapon of the Liberal party. I agree it is possibly the strongest weapon in Moral Re-Armament. But at least, after deliberating and hearing some of these arguments on Moral Re-Armament the committee decided that although it might be a consistent policy it was not suitable for discussion.
So that all in all I think this government has been very consistent in its defence policy. Certainly the committee had every opportunity to discuss policy, and used that opportunity, and I think the Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Trinity have been less than honest in stating that there was no time given to the members of the opposition to discuss questions of policy or to ask questions about policy.

I wish to correct one of the statements made by the hon. member who has just resumed his seat. I did not produce any book put out by Moral Re-Armament in the committee. It was a NATO handbook published by General Carpentier retired commander of allied forces in central Europe.
And leader of Moral ReArmament too?

Before this item carries I should like to make a few comments on the speech we heard from the hon. member for Trinity, with the refusal of members of the Liberal party to consider in its proper aspect the Bomarc weapon and the reason for the existence of this weapon. I should also like to comment on what the hon. member said concerning NORAD. I heard the hon. member for Trinity mention that according to his information in the second half of the sixties such weapons as the Bomarc would become completely useless.
The hon. member was no doubt basing this statement on the fact that in his opinion missile development would then have reached such a stage that the main threat would be from intercontinental ballistic missiles rather than from any other form of weapon. I should like to remind the hon. member that though there may be a certain validity in this, though in the second half of the sixties the threat of a missile attack will be intensified, the fact still remains that there will be a gap of five years during which we could expect an attack by manned bombers, and I should like to remind the hon. member of the fact that the Bomarc surface to air missile as well as the interceptor are weapons which are meant to defend our country against the possibility of such an attack by manned bombers.
Surely the hon. member for Trinity, who obviously has given a great deal of study

to defence matters, would not suggest to this committee or to the people of Canada that we should be left completely defenceless during those five years. Surely the hon. member must know that the Bomarc program is an integrated program which has been put together by the best military brains of both the United States and Canada. The purpose of this program is to protect our main centres and especially our strategic air command bases against the possibility of an attack by manned bombers. It is a program which is conducted on a co-operative basis, not a program which is conducted on a purely Canadian basis. In other words we have not decided here in Canada to have just two stations which will perform in solitary splendour. The function of this weapon is to protect two regions in Quebec and Ontario. Other stations are meant to protect the maritime regions and other densely populated sectors in the eastern area.
Surely, Mr. Chairman, it is rather futile to call useless a program on which so much money has been spent and into which so much effort has been put. I should like once again to remind the committee that a sum well in excess of $2,300 million has been spent in order to render effective this Bomarc weapon, and truly,-
Will the minister permit a question?
Yes.
Will the minister say that the amount of money which has been sunk in a program is any criterion of its future usefulness?

If you consider the well
known competence of our southern neighbours it will become quite obvious that if they had considered this program was of no use at all they most certainly would have stopped the spending of those enormous sums of money well before spending the fabulous sum of $2,300 million. The very fact that they decided to carry on this program is indicated by the repeated successes which we have witnessed quite recently at the Bomarc B trials. Surely, Mr. Chairman, if the Bomarc B effort is some measure of defence against the possibility of a manned bomber attack, if those Bomarc B's succeeded in destroying some of the attacking bombers, surely the installation of these Bomarc B stations are worth the sum of money which we in Canada are asked to spend on this particular weapon.
I repeat, the sum of money which we shall be called upon to spend on the installation of the Bomarc B stations is only $12 million which in relation to the sum of money which
Supply-National Defence our powerful neighbours will spend is truly not too much. Furthermore, I must bring to your attention a very serious contradiction which we have noticed in the hon. member's so-called bold program for national defence. On the one hand he advocates the complete elimination of the Bomarc stations, and he also advocates that we dispense with the development of the installation called SAGE. In other words, he would like to scrap everything and yet another part of this bold program is to replace the CF-100 by another interceptor. I certainly will not go against this suggestion which I think has its merits, and which is being studied; but I should like to draw to the attention of the committee the fact that these new interceptors, which the hon. member in his new bold program would like to see in Canada, could hardly be effective and operational without the existence of this installation called SAGE. How can he on the one hand ask for the scrapping of the SAGE installations, and on the other hand ask that we purchase or use interceptors which can hardly be operational unless we have these very SAGE installations?
I should also like to comment on what I heard the hon. member say about NORAD. I do not know who the great military advisers of the hon. member can be who advise this policy of scrapping our ships, scrapping Bomarc, scrapping this and scrapping that at the same time as we increase or keep at the same level the national budget. But surely those advisers cannot be as clever or as competent as those men who are actually at the present time protecting us at NORAD. The officials and senior officers of NORAD are the most experienced officers of the United States and the Canadian services, and they are trying to provide for this country, for this continent in fact, the very best defence that can be devised. I for one, and I feel that the majority of the members of the committee will join me in this, have far more confidence in the military valour and the military knowledge of those men who are guiding the destinies of NORAD than I have in the military advisers of the hon. member for Trinity or, if he has no advisers, in his own strategic and tactical competence in service matters. I do not believe that the hon. member for Trinity, nor the colleagues of the hon. member who sit in the official opposition ranks, are really serving the interests of Canada by deliberately belittling the efforts of those who at NORAD are contributing so much to the defence of this continent.
Before I resume my seat I should like to say I am shocked, as most members of the committee and as most sane thinking Canadians must be at the present time, at the

Supply-National Defence realization that this so-called glamorous and bold defence policy which has been dinned into our ears since we started this session and for quite a while before resolves itself into the suggestion that we scrap everything, that we build nothing and that we completely eliminate all defences, thus leaving the North American continent and this nation exposed to a vicious and violent attack from our potential enemy.
If the hon. member for Trinity, his advisers, his colleagues and the Leader of the Opposition had come forth today with constructive suggestions, which would possibly give us a chance to improve our defences, the defences of this country, and our policies for the protection of our citizens, I can assure them that we on this side of the house would have been the first to accept those suggestions, because we fully realize that the problem of defence is away beyond and above political controversy; but it is truly almost shameful to think that hon. members of the opposition have deliberately deceived the Canadian people by making them believe-
Be careful, now.

Mr. Chairman, on a point of order, not only has the minister just presented the house with a bald, unadulterated lie in his interpretation of what we have put forward in this debate, but he has imputed motives in saying that we deliberately deceived-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I think that the minister went beyond the rules of the house in saying that the members of the opposition had deliberately deceived the people of Canada but I think that the hon. member for Trinity was equally guilty in using the words he used. Therefore I think the two hon. members should correct their remarks.
On the point of order, Mr. Chairman, if the minister will relate all the positive programs we put forward in our policy, I will withdraw what I said.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I did not put any condition on my demand, and I am sure that both hon. members will correct their statements unconditionally.

Mr. Chairman, I admit that possibly the expression I used went a bit too far and was not quite parliamentary. I therefore withdraw the words "deliberately deceived", but I do not think that even the well known susceptibility of the hon. member for Trinity, which has been tried so frequently during the last two days, will be offended if I say instead that they were
[Mr. Sevigny.l

possibly inadvertently deluded into the belief that they had a policy. The fact of the matter is, Mr. Chairman-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. As far as the point of order is concerned, as the minister has withdrawn the expression he used, which was objectionable, I think we should give the hon. member for Trinity a chance to do the same.

Mr. Chairman, on the basis that the minister has withdrawn his imputation with respect to motives I will withdraw what I said except in respect of the minister inadvertently having left out of his appreciation of the policy we put forward all of the positive alternatives we have placed before the house and the country for consideration as opposed to the present policies of the government of Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: It was you who left them out.

Mr. Chairman, I accept the withdrawal of the hon. member for Trinity. I appreciate the fact that he also accepted my withdrawal, and I shall continue. As I was saying, it seems that hon. members opposite were inadvertently deluded into the belief that they had a constructive policy, and they actually raised a great hue and cry over this great policy that they were going to offer. I confess that I for one was quite anxious to hear what this great policy was going to be. I must say that I read with interest yesterday what appeared in the Citizen and which the hon. member repeated afterwards in the house most eloquently.
But I was shocked to see that this so-called bold, illuminating defence policy which was being offered to the committee contained almost nothing except some suggestions that we possibly could carry on with a course that we had already explained to the house we were trying to follow. It seems to me, that to criticize when actually it is almost admitted that there is not much to criticize, to put before the country the view that everything is wrong, that everything is just going to pot, that we are defenceless, that we have nothing-
You said it.

-that the leaders of the government and the service chiefs and so on do not know anything; to say that they and their advisers know it all and will eventually come forward with a great Liberal policy and then to produce nothing is, I must frankly say, a shameful waste of the time of the committee and is certainly not the way to serve the Canadian people who must have confidence in those who are entrusted with

the responsibility for defence and who certainly deserve better than the rather inane and inept suggestions we have heard in this defence policy.
(Translation):
Mr. Chairman, closing my remarks in French, may I recall an old saying to the effect that when one has nothing to say and nothing to suggest, it is better not to say anything. In other words, one should not waste the time of the House of Commons of the Canadian parliament, and it is certainly better, on such an important subject as national defence, to keep a respectful silence with regard to the able and efficient work done by those who are responsible for protecting the Canadian nation, rather than to waste the time of so many people with inept statements such as those we heard in the speeches made by the members of the official opposition since we began consideration of the Department of National Defence estimates.
(Text):

Mr. Chairman, this debate seems to have accomplished a great deal so far by introducing a positive, constructive alternative to the government's waffling and lack of policy in defence matters. We have at least provoked a debate on the subject of national defence and 1 think that in itself is very worth while. Not only that, we have brought out of the closet the Associate Minister of National Defence and this we welcome. This is a development of some importance.
The minister, who until now has been in relative obscurity, has come forward at last, stood on his feet and said something about national defence. For a long while we heard nothing at all from him. The special committee on defence expenditures met for 27 days, but where was the Associate Minister of National Defence during all that time? Why was he not at the side of the Minister of National Defence during those meetings? Where was he? Was he closeted somewhere? What was he doing? Why was he not there to answer questions and to listen to and take part in the discussion so that he would be as familiar with these matters as other hon. members are? We could never figure out what had happened to the Associate Minister of National Defence.
On the second last day of the committee's meetings the Minister of National Defence could not be there and a very able departmental official answered questions for us. But the Associate Minister of National Defence could have been there to substitute for the minister on that occasion and we regret that he was not able to take the time to do so. Up to now all we had heard about
Supply-National Defence him was that he had gone to the city of Toronto and had taken a prepared speech with him about the Avro Arrow which he read to a Progressive Conservative businessmen's group. What did he say? He started off by saying that he had prepared the speech. The same speech had been made a few days before to the defence expenditures committee by the Minister of National Defence who also said that he had prepared the speech. One of them had had a lapse of memory. I do not know which one it was but obviously they both could not have prepared the same speech.
Maybe they both agreed.

The speech he has made today was not the same. It was longer but at least it was not the same. We welcome this emergence of the butterfly from the cocoon. Now the Associate Minister of National Defence has come forward in the house and has begun to make himself heard. This is a worth-while development and we hope we will hear a great deal more from him in the days and weeks that lie ahead. However, he still has not learned about some of the fine points. I appreciate the difficulty he has but this is really no excuse. With reference to NORAD, for instance, he has said that the military officers of NORAD are pre-eminent. They are excellent officers who do their jobs in a most efficient fashion.
It is high time you said so.

They are first-class officers, but I feel sorry for them in the environment in which they are working. They have not been given a chance either by the Canadian or the United States governments. The future that faces them, in view of the lack of effective defence against intercontinental ballistic missiles, is a bleak one and puts them under the difficulties which that situation creates. The Minister of National Defence has said that we should listen to their advice. He and his government did not listen to their advice. They advised the Canadian government to go ahead with the Avro Arrow.
How do you know that?

They said we should have defence interceptor squadrons. They came to Ottawa to try to persuade the Canadian government to go ahead with the production in Canada of long range interceptors. What did the Canadian government do about it? They did absolutely nothing. Why then, if you value this advice so much, do you not take it, or do you not believe it? Do you feel your judgment is better than theirs? If you do, why do you question anyone else who differs with them?

Supply-National Dejence
Even within military circles there is no unanimity. This is inevitable when you reach a state of change in military atfairs such as we presently have before us. You are not going to get complete agreement amongst all people. How would you expect to do that? There is even disagreement amongst the United States forces themselves. The air force in the Pentagon does not agree completely with the NORAD commander in chief. If the hon. gentleman had taken the trouble to read the evidence presented before the house and senate committees of the United States he would know that. NORAD has asked for all sorts of things, and the chief of the air force said, we cannot give it to you; we do not feel it is a justifiable expenditure of the public funds of the United States under these circumstances. Surely the hon. gentleman recognizes, then, that it is not unreasonable for someone else to stand up and question any other recommendations made by the same command in respect of the expenditure of the public funds of Canada.
This is especially true, after this program was knocked out by congress, in its wisdom. Congress had no confidence in it. They listened not only to General White, the chief of the air force, but they listened to General Kuter. They were so interested in what General White has said about the Bomarc-SAGE system, and that created so many questions in their minds, that they wanted to call General Kuter in order to get his personal views. They got General Kuter to come to Washington and present his case, present the problems of his command and put forward his requests. They listened to those views, but they did not accept them. General Kuter did not get anything like what he asked for before the house and senatorial committees. The associate minister should at least know that. So, obviously the senate, congress, the air force, the joint chiefs of staff in the United States and the president disagreed with what the NORAD chief had requested. They all thought that under the existing circumstances and the available amount of public funds there were uses to which the money could be put which would be more in the public interest than fulfilling the total requirements of that command. Yet the minister has the audacity to come in here this afternoon and suggest that anyone who differs with a military commander is out of order.
This is a strange policy and a strange suggestion now on the part of the associate minister. Then, Mr. Chairman, the piece de resistance, is that the associate minister says that for five years at least the threat of the bomber is the great thing.
Can you deny it?

We are going to hear something about the great unanimity on the other side of the house now. This is not what the Minister of National Defence said in this committee last year on July 2, 1959 when defence estimates were being considered. As reported at page 5350 of Hansard for that date, the minister said:
In the early 1960's it is expected that the ballistic missiles will have reached a stage of reliability whereby such missiles will replace the bombers as the primary means of delivering nuclear weapons on North America.
In the early 1960's the minister said that missiles would replace the bombers as the primary means of delivering nuclear weapons on North America.
That does not mean there is no threat from bombers.

I continue the quotation:
However, if an attack on this continent is made in the early 1960's it is considered quite probable that a variety of weapons would be used in an effort to saturate the defences and thus deliver a devastating attack.
This kind of attack would include ballistic missiles, both long and short range, land based or from submarines, as well as other nuclear weapons delivered by aircraft. As most of the major strategic targets are situated in the United States it is more than likely that certain targets in Canada would be attacked by bombers, although the primary threat would be from the ICBM's.
This is the Minister of National Defence saying that in the early 1960's the primary threat will shift from the manned bomber to the intercontinental ballistic missiles and other missiles. Does the associate minister disagree with the view expressed by the Minister of National Defence on that occasion?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: There is no difference in what he said.

Does he deny that two or three years hence this will be much more so, that the total capacity at that time of intercontinental ballistic missiles will be three, four -I do not know how many times-what it is at present? Does the minister deny this? Does he deny that under those circumstances, in the event of an all-out war in which Russia chooses to attack, first, that all the major targets on the North American continent-yes, even all the major cities and all the Bomarc sites could be obliterated with the first blow. Does he deny that? If he does, let him rise in his place and say so.
You denied it yourself yesterday.

If he does not deny it, then why does he say a couple of Bomarc squadrons will make any difference by the mid-1960's and beyond?
Furthermore, he said the interceptors we had recommended for the identification role would not be effective without the SAGE system. Can the minister tell us if the SAGE system is presently in operation, and if this is necessary for the CF-lOO's? If it is, why has the minister these nine squadrons in existence at the present time? Does the minister deny that aircraft can carry its own radar? Does the minister deny that an aircraft can work independently of SAGE under any circumstances? Even if he should deny that, what possible use, under some circumstances at least with an all-out attack, which is what we are considering, would the SAGE system be when it is soft, when it has a whole mass of electronic equipment on top of the ground which could be knocked out with one grenade or one missile.

It would have to be a big
grenade.
Yes, it would, but it would not take much of a grenade to knock out an electronic computer of that complexity, and the minister knows it.

Mr. Chairman, I have listened with great interest to the eloquent expose of the hon. member for Trinity. I should like to explain very briefly a few personal things in answer to what he said. It is quite true that I have not risen too frequently in this house, but there is a reason for this. I do not believe I should rise in my place unless I have something specific to say. I would suggest to the hon. member for Trinity that if he observed this principle that there is strength and beauty in silence he would not have exposed this committee to the gentle, but always inept, nonsense we have heard from him since this session started. It is really rather amusing in a way, Mr. Chairman, but also rather boring in another, to think that so much time of this house has been wasted by the hon. member for Trinity.
Why do you not talk about the issues?

But eventually at one time he decided to come out with this nonsense that we heard yesterday in this lengthy speech of his. Speaking of speeches, the hon. member referred to a speech which I made in Toronto a few months ago. He claims that I took this speech with me and that I went to Toronto and made such a speech. Mr. Chairman, I can tell you this-and the hon. member for Trinity can ask all those people from Toronto who heard me-that I went there and spoke without notes. I did not read my speech; I delivered my remarks, and those remarks were actually prepared by myself and said by myself; they were not prepared by anyone else or said by someone else.

Mr. Chairman, before we pass this item I should like to answer some of the questions which have been raised during this two-day debate. First of all, I should like to express my appreciation to all those who have taken part in discussing this very vital subject of national defence. I am quite certain that all who have spoken have done so in a sincere and determined effort to try to present their views-the ones that they held for some considerable time-before this committee so that in trying to solve these extremely difficult problems that the Department of National Defence is faced with we might have the benefit of the considered opinions that have been held, or that are held, by the various parties and groups in this house and by the various individuals themselves.
I think it is quite evident from what has been said so far during this debate that all members are deeply concerned about the future, and what the future may hold, should conditions in the world become so grave that war would break out again. I want to assure all members of this committee that the government is exerting its utmost endeavours to secure a lasting peace. Nobody has been more sincere or more persistent in his efforts to further the international discussions which are going on, and have been going on during this summer, in order to try to solve what seems to be the almost insoluble problem of how to settle international differences, than has the Secretary of State for External Affairs who has had the support of all members of

this government. I am certain that all hon. members hope that our endeavours will meet with success.
It has been quite clear during the debate that the terrible consequences of another world war are obvious to all members, and it is because of the importance and the complexity of the problem that sincere points of view have been expressed, and at times during the discussions some heat has been generated.
We face an international situation which has deteriorated in the last two months. Everyone had high hopes a short time ago that some definite progress would have been made during the summit conference. We have been proponents in furthering the ideas of disarmament at the conference in Geneva. But we have to be realistic. While there is sabre rattling on the other side of the iron curtain, while threats are being made as to what may happen in the next few months in Berlin and in other parts of Europe, while the soviets, we are told, are making great progress with the development of modern weapons and their army, air force and navy are equipped with such weapons as have never been seen before, as Mr. Khrushchev stated not very many months ago, we cannot let down our guard entirely. We are not aggressors. We know not when a war may be started by a very powerful and ruthless government which gives indications of being ready to start aggression at almost any time.
That faces defence planners with a problem, the magnitude of which can hardly be realized. Are we to plan today for the possibility of a war breaking out later this year or next year or can we say that the indications are such that we may set aside the defences of the moment, that we may set aside the steps which are being taken to prevent war now and make preparations solely for a war which might take place ten years hence?
It seems to me that while we all agree that every effort must be made to prevent war there is a difference of opinion as to the best steps to be taken to prevent that war. Some members have expressed the opinion that war is so unlikely at the present time that it is not necessary for us to protect ourselves against the possibility of a bomber attack. Others have indicated that they feel that if war did break out in the near future bombers would be used. In giving evidence before the committee I made this statement as my considered opinion:
As far as ICBM's are concerned, the Russians have, undoubtedly, some such missiles operational and within the next few years they will probably have several hundred available. As their missile capability increases, less and less reliance will be placed on their bombers.

We were faced with that decision a couple of years ago when, owing to the heavy expense involved in producing and completing the development of what would have been a superb interceptor, the CF-105, had the production been completed, we decided that the cost was too high and we did not feel we were then justified in spending that amount of money on this particular weapon to defend the country against the bomber. The committee resumed at 8 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose at six o'clock we were discussing the air defence of the North American continent and in particular the amount of the appropriation which has been allocated to these operations. I had pointed out that while there might not be any immediate threat of a planned war, still there was a possibility of war coming by accident or misadventure, and if war did come within the next few years it was inevitable that the Russians would employ their bombers against targets on this continent. It is realized that the percentage of the threat as compared with bomber to missile is increasing in favour of the missile. But still there exists a bomber threat. Therefore the problem which faces the government is to decide how much effort should be placed into the defence against the bomber should it occur in the next few years.
The government's position is that while the primary threat will gradually be swinging towards the missile, there is still a threat from the many hundred bombers in the Russian air force. Therefore we should take some precautions in order to help protect the SAC bomber bases of the retaliatory force located in the United States, and the major industrial cities. To do this we had decided to join with the United States in providing two Bomarc sites, one at North Bay and one at La Macaza, and to have these equipped with the Bomarc B, with a limited number of missiles, at a cost to Canada for the construction of those bases of some $12 million.
The Liberals, in presenting their program, while they realized that there was a danger of war occurring by misadventure, and realized that if that did occur within the next few years bombers would be used against targets in North America, prefer to use interceptors rather than to rely mainly on the Bomarcs as far as the Canadian contribution was concerned. The C.C.F. proposal was that we should discontinue the Bomarc and not replace it with interceptors, but rely entirely on the retaliatory forces of the United States and, I presume, the interceptor squadrons also

based in the United States. The government cannot accept that recommendation of the C.C.F. party, because we do believe that there is a possibility of bomber war, and because we are in a partnership with the United States and should play our fair share.
Regarding the Liberal proposal, I think their recommendation was based on two main facts. First of all, they dislike the use of nuclear weapons and they feel that the Bomarc will be fired from a fixed site and therefore will present a vulnerable target to hostile missile attack. I should like to discuss those two problems for just a minute. They recommended doing away with the Bomarc, cancelling the construction which is now going on at the two sites.
Regarding the first factor which influenced them, namely the use of nuclear warheads, the Bomarc cannot obtain its full effectiveness unless it is equipped with a nuclear warhead. Nor would interceptors be able to carry out their full effectiveness unless they also were equipped with nuclear weapons. And if pilots of the R.C.A.F. were flying interceptors which were not armed with nuclear weapons, they would be inferiorly armed in relation to the United States air force squadrons which would also be flying in Canadian air space if bombers were attacking this North American continent. Those interceptors of the United States air force would be equipped with nuclear weapons.
As far as the question of fixed bases is concerned, of course the Bomarcs are at a fixed site. Their launchers would be stationary. But I do suggest that as the Bomarc is only a weapon to be used against bombers, it is unlikely that the Russians during that period when it may be expected they would use bombers against us, when their number of missiles would be comparatively limited, could devote some of those missiles against a target which was designed purely to defeat the bomber.

I am sorry, but there are a number of questions which I do feel I should answer, and also reply to some of the statements which have been made.
The fixed bases of the Bomarc are so small that I think it will be most unlikely that a missile fired from 3,000 to 4,000 miles away would be able to obtain a hit or would 79951-0-483
Supply-National Defence have those sites selected as a target. Of course, one must remember that the jet aircraft must take off from air fields with a comparatively long runway, and I am not at all sure that the air fields capable of supporting jet interceptors would not be just as vulnerable a target as the Bomarc sites. So I really do not see that there is a great deal of argument on that score. We must remember that these two sites are located north of the great industrial cities of eastern Canada and while their primary purpose may be the protection of the SAC bomber bases, they will still offer a considerable degree of protection to the cities in eastern Canada.
Then there is one other point I would like to make in connection with the proposal of the Liberal party in this respect, and that is that it is very much more expensive of course to maintain interceptor squadrons than it is to maintain the Bomarc sites. As I pointed out, Bomarc sites would cost $12 million to $15 million. The number of missiles we may assume to be approximately 30 on each site. As a basis of calculation which has been accepted in the United States, one interceptor would cost the equivalent of three missiles. That would mean that if we were going to replace the missiles with interceptors we should require 180 interceptors to replace the 60 Bomarc missiles. Each of those interceptors might possibly cost about $2 million apiece.
So you see, Mr. Chairman, you would be running up an expense of some $360 million as opposed to the $12 million which the government proposes to spend on the Bomarc missile. Then of course maintenance of the interceptor squadrons is far greater than the maintenance of the Bomarc sites and the number of personnel which are required to man the interceptor squadrons is much greater. The Leader of the Opposition did say that it might not be necessary to employ as many interceptors as there are now being employed in the nine squadrons, so perhaps he does not anticipate using that full number of 180. Actually, today we have considerably more CF-lOO's in our squadrons and reserves than the 180.
Another factor comes up here, and that is that I am very doubtful whether there are available in the United States this number of interceptors which could be obtained readily. Again, it may be-and this was not clear in the remarks which were made-that perhaps they are considering primarily that these interceptors would be used merely for identification and recognition purposes. As I have indicated the government has under consideration the possibility of replacing

Supply-National Defence some of the CF-lOO's with a limited number of interceptors which could be used for recognition purposes.
Now regarding SAGE, which the Liberals recommended should also be discontinued, SAGE is required. If any interceptors or reconnaissance aircraft, be they for identification or recognition, are flying at supersonic speeds, all United States air force interceptors are equipped with radar which will operate with the SAGE environment. SAGE is being installed from the Atlantic to the Pacific and if we discontinued the one SAGE installation which we are putting in in Canada there will be no opportunity of controlling and guiding the United States interceptors which might in the absence of our own interceptors, or joining with our own interceptors if we had them, do battle in Canadian skies. So I do suggest that it is imperative whether we go ahead with the Bomarc or not that the SAGE environment should be continued and I could not accept the recommendation of the Liberal party that the SAGE environment be discontinued.
The Leader of the Opposition asked questions regarding the negotiations going on in connection with the acquisition of nuclear warheads. We have had a lot of discussion about that and I should have though that the position of the government was clear. We are entering into and have been carrying on discussions at various levels, the official level and between Canadian ministers and United States ministers, as to the sort of arrangement which could be made when nuclear warheads are made available which, as the Prime Minister said, will be so if and when they are required. We recognize, and 1 am sure the Leader of the Opposition does also, that by United States law these nuclear warheads whenever they leave the United States must still remain the property of the United States. So whether these warheads are placed in Canada or in the leased bases in Canada or in the United Kingdom, the United States still retain possession of them until such time as the President of the United States releases them for use to the authorities of the country concerned.
In the United Kingdom where these nuclear weapons are now stored a form of joint control is exercised whereby a United States officer has a key to the receptacle where they are stored and also a British officer has a key, and the door cannot be opened unless both keys are used. So you have a form of joint control not dissimilar to the method which is used by anybody having a safety deposit box in the bank where the banker has one key and the lessee of the box has the other.


There would seem to be no difficulties in the way of reaching some sort of similar agreement regarding the storage of those nuclear weapons on Canadian soil. Then when the situation becomes such that these weapons are to be used, the sole authority to authorize the use of those weapons in Canada would be the Prime Minister of Canada who, having had them released by the President of the United States, would then give directions as to when and how they should be actually used.

Would the minister permit a question on that point? Could the minister tell us how much warning we would have of an international intercontinental ballistic missile during which this joint control would have to operate?

The immediate amount of warning would be approximately 30 minutes but there might be several days of warning. It does not necessarily follow that the first missile would be fired against the Canadian target. It is quite likely or it is quite possible, shall I say, that the first missiles might fall in the United States, thereby giving us, perhaps, hours of warning. It is inconceivable in the present stage of the development of missilry that all the Russian missiles could be fired off simultaneously. So when I say the minimum amount of warning would be 30 minutes, there might be considerably more warning than that.
That, I hope, explains the present position. There are these discussions going on. We have not got the launchers yet. We do not expect the launchers until some time next year, and I am quite certain that the Secretary of State for External Affairs will be able to complete the negotiations by that date so that as the Prime Minister has said these weapons will be available if and when required. But, as the Leader of the Opposition knows full well, there are negotiations; at least there are vigorous demands being made by numerous countries to ban the use of nuclear weapons altogether. If these are successful, and if it is generally agreed that nuclear weapons shall not be used, then, thank God, we shall not have to have them. I hope that answers your question. I think that is all I had on continental defence.
Now we come to the question of mobile forces of conventional arms. Great stress was made by the Liberal spokesmen on the importance of having a mobile force capable of being transported by air to practically any part of the world where it might be necessary for Canadian forces to operate in support of some United Nations project. I heartily agree,

and I said very definitely in my opening remarks that we attach importance to the provision of additional air transport for that very purpose. As a matter of fact, there is part of the total of $170 million included in this year's estimates for the purpose of acquiring additional air transport. I have already mentioned the types of air transport there are- the CC-106, the CC-109 and the 130-B. The most recent order we have placed is for the Caribou to operate in the Congo. Thus I do feel we have during the last three years built up the air transport command, and certainly before the end of this financial year the majority of these aircraft will have been delivered and we shall be in a position to move three or four times the number of troops, together with their equipment. The aircraft known as 130-B move a very great quantity of equipment, much heavier equipment than it has ever been possible for us to move before, and with this combination of air transport in air transport command we shall be by the end of this fiscal year in a very strong position to move troops as required.
I have repeatedly mentioned the stand-by battalion. Yes, there is a battalion composed of approximately 1,000 men ready to move at any time. It is not the fault of Canada that in the particular situation arising in the Congo a different type of troops were required, emphasis being laid on staff officers, signal communication troops and what is usually referred to as logistic troops, supply personnel and so on. Some of these troops were already immunized and could have been moved into the Congo earlier than they actually were, but the difficulty was for the Congo United Nations force to decide exactly what type of personnel were required.
Canada supplied the first staff officers to the Congo force. We have ten trained staff officers in the Congo now providing a very essential element to the commander, including his chief of staff. Less than half an hour ago I signed an order for six more officers to join that force. Canada is ready to meet the modest requests that have been made to her.
It is suggested we should have a brigade instead of a battalion. That is just a question of emphasis. I doubt whether it will be practical for us to have and maintain an air transport force capable of moving a full brigade in a very short time. I am doubtful whether a situation would arise whereby the United Nations would call upon Canada to make such a large contribution, and if they did we have three brigades here in Canada of trained, regular soldiers who in a short time could be made available for any further United Nations operations.
