The suggestion was made by the hon. member for Trinity that we should have a troopcarrying supply ship to go to distant places where air transport could not take troops. I find it rather difficult to visualize such territory where it would be more expeditious to put a large number of troops into a ship to move quickly to some point, where you could not reach that point, or near that point, with air transport. I cannot help feeling that it would be preferable to continue what we are doing and to maintain a strong transport command. Therefore, I feel in principle we are not widely distant; it is just a question of degree in that respect.
The Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Trinity both emphasized the importance of increasing the mobility of the brigade in Europe. As hon. members know, we have a brigade group there. Last year we entirely motorized that brigade. We provided enough motor vehicles, adding 41 motor vehicles to each battalion, so the whole force could be moved in motor vehicles. I know that these are not amphibian vehicles but there is not a brigade in Europe, unless perhaps some of the United States brigades so equipped, and I do not know that they are equipped with carriers. We have been in the forefront of the development of an armoured amphibian motor vehicle for the carrying of personnel. That vehicle is in its final stages of testing. Actually the last information that I received indicates that the final complete tests will be finished next month, and when we get these final tests, if the vehicle comes up to expectation, it is the intention to go into production of that vehicle so that it will to a very large extent meet the requirements which were suggested by the Leader of the Opposition and others.
He did suggest helicopters. Yes, helicopters would be useful, but helicopters are not generally detailed down to brigade formation. While we have some helicopters with the air division in Europe which, if necessity arose, could be allocated to the brigade group, and I believe have taken part in some of the exercises which have been conducted by that brigade group, we have not yet seen our way clear to providing the helicopters which are necessary. To be quite frank with the committee, we have been investigating the very knotty problem as to what type of helicopter should be used. We would like to have one type of helicopter which could be used by all the three forces, the navy, the army and the air force. It does not seem quite practical that we can do that. If we could get all the forces to accept one type of helicopter and could have enough orders to justify that helicopter being manufactured in Canada that would be the ideal situation.

Supply-National Defence Failing that we may have to purchase helicopters from the United States. There is a small air element attached to the brigade for artillery reconnaissance and for intercommunication between the various units of the brigade for commanders, and so forth.
Now, I must absolutely refute the suggestion that the brigade is equipped with obsolescent weapons and that it is not well equipped. I do not believe that there is one weapon in the brigade which an infantry brigade of the Canadian forces used during world war II. They have all been replaced by more modern and more up to date types. The primary weapon, the rifle, has been completely changed. They have the C-l, the C-2 the FN rifle. There are new mortars, new wireless equipment and so forth. My parliamentary secretary put on the record last night a list of the new equipment that is being used, and I would emphasize the fact that the centurion tanks which they now have are being fitted up with armour-protected gasoline tanks, and their armament is being increased with a heavier and more up-to-date gun. Therefore, I feel that it is not fair, it is not a just criticism and not fair to the troops to say that they are not equipped with up to date weapons.
A question was asked yesterday regarding research. We have been able to spend only a limited amount of money on research, but our research programs have been as extensive as the staff of scientists of the defence research board could cope with. As one hon. member said yesterday, one of the big troubles has been the pay of the scientists in the government service.
There has been a tremendous demand for scientists in industry, and unless they are dedicated men, many have found it much more profitable to take positions in industry. But I think hon. members know-at least those who were on the committee do know -that there was an increase in the salaries of scientists in the defence research board authorized last June. Previously the minimum wage for scientists was $5,000; that has been increased to $5,240. The maximum was $14,500; that has been increased to $16,500. We hope that this will go some way toward stabilizing in their positions the scientists that we now have. There is a slight increase in the vote for research and I hope it will be possible to expend the full amount.
A question was asked about navigational aids and infra-red equipment which would enable tanks and vehicles to operate at night. The defence research board and the army have been working together on what are known as the navigational aid and infra-red projects. The navigational aids are under unit test now and have been lent to the

United States and to the United Kingdom. We have recommended to the NATO organization that these weapons be included in the likely projects which all countries of NATO were asked to submit in the expectation that they would be accepted by all the nations. Therefore I feel that in that respect we are making progress and I hope this information will be of interest to the hon. member who asked the question.
A question was asked by the Leader of the Opposition, I believe, regarding the use of nuclear weapons by NATO. He asked whether it was the policy of NATO to use nuclear weapons in what would be mainly a land war in Europe. While, as the hon. member knows full well, it is not possible to disclose all details regarding the use of equipment by NATO forces because the information is classified by NATO, I have a quotation from a speech made by General Norstad, the supreme allied commander, at the University of Southern California on December 6 in which he said:
The forces which are assigned to the NATO mission are after all largely organized around nuclear weapons; the defence of Europe against a serious attack depends on these weapons.
The suggestion has been made that we should not use nuclear weapons in Europe if enemy forces start an invasion of western Europe and that we should rely on conventional arms to repulse such an invasion. It is my opinion that NATO does not have sufficient strength in personnel and conventional arms to be able to resist an attack by Russian forces which would be supported by their conventional arms and, as we know, the Russian army is equipped with tactical nuclear weapons. If our soldiers are to have a fighting chance should they be attacked I feel it is imperative that they should have the use of nuclear weapons in the same way that the soldiers of the other allied countries will have nuclear weapons released to them through the NATO commander.

I wonder whether the minister would permit two questions before he leaves that particular subject. It was the reading of General Norstad's statement that inspired my question to the minister, and I was wondering whether the NATO council had ever confirmed his statement that nuclear weapons would be used. If the minister does not feel it is appropriate to answer my second question I will understand, but I should like to know whether all the other members of NATO have agreed to accept tactical nuclear weapons for their defence.

I think I would be justified in saying that the principle of the employment of nuclear weapons has been accepted by the

NATO council. I would not feel justified in saying whether all have accepted it but the principle has been accepted and these nuclear weapons, as a matter of fact, are placed in Europe now.
In some countries.

Some of them, and they would still have to be released by the President of the United States to the supreme allied commander before he would have the authority to use them. I do not say necessarily a few minutes before. There may be conditions set under which he may use them that I would not know, but they would have to be released by the President of the United States.
A question was asked whether our 104 squadrons would use nuclear weapons. All I can say there is that they would have the capability of using these weapons. Whether they would be allowed to operate with them from French bases I do not know. I am sure the Leader of the Opposition is aware of all the discussion there has been about that matter. That would have to be arranged by the NATO supreme allied commander with the French government and, in any event, we have air bases in Germany as well as in France. That is a problem which will have to be faced when the new aircraft become available.
I cannot accept the suggestions made by the hon. member for Trinity about the unsuitability of the 104. As I said the day before yesterday, the 104 has been chosen by other NATO countries for this dual role, and after the most careful investigation we decided it was the most suitable aircraft. I know that for various reasons the hon. member for Trinity does not like that particular aircraft, but we had to make a decision and we have decided that it is a good aircraft. Only minor modifications are being made to it. Nothing like new development is being done, as the hon. member suggested. It is not a wholly new project. Only minor alterations are being made. It is a proved type and, as I said before, Belgium, Holland, Germany and Italy have all accepted that aircraft and I believe other countries are also accepting it.
One hon. member raised a question about manpower cuts. I think I made it quite clear that as long as Canada has commitments for her armed forces, which we have accepted, there can be no substantial reduction in the number of the forces. I have said that over and over again. While it was mentioned today that I had said we were looking into the question of reducing the numbers, I stressed the point that in my previous statements I have said there would be no substantial cuts. We are always looking for ways whereby we can economize, particularly in manpower and
Supply-National Defence particularly in the administrative branch, be it military or civilian personnel. I am fully aware of the fact that for general economic reasons we cannot expect any large increase in the defence budget, and we find costs of operation, costs of maintenance, costs of personnel, always going up, as well as the costs of acquiring new equipment. It is difficult to adjust these. We do, therefore, regularly examine all our establishments to see if there can be any reductions there.
One other question was asked and that was connected with survival operations. The hon. member asked if the militia were receiving training equipment for survival operations. As I mentioned yesterday, the militia is doing admirable work in these survival operations. I do attach a great deal of importance both to the training of the regular and militia units. While it is not possible to obtain much of the equipment, because it is not procurable at the present time and there is not sufficient money to get all the equipment which the troops could use, we are getting enough training equipment and a good deal of operational equipment as well, both for the regular forces and the militia.
I think I have covered most of the points which were raised. If I have left out any, perhaps hon. members would ask the questions when we are considering the other votes and I have the officials here to fill in the details.

Might I ask the minister a second question while they are en route. I have a couple of letters from people at Robert's Creek claiming that buildings have been damaged and windows broken as a result of concussion consequent upon firing practice by the navy. Has the minister received any complaints in that respect, and what is the usual procedure to make certain people's property is not damaged and that they do not suffer any unnecessary inconvenience?

Have there been any claims paid in connection with damage caused by concussion from gunfire?

I wonder if the hon. member would be kind enough to repeat his first question so that he may get an answer to it?

Certainly, I think it would be just as well if I sent the letter over to the minister. I do not want to take the time of the committee to read it. I will start where I left off. It was brought up, I believe, in the estimates committee of the Department of National Health and Welfare that the milita would take over and assist the civil defence program in time of emergency. For the last three years our militia unit in Kimberley has been having great difficulty, especially with their accommodation. I received a letter from the Kimberley organization a little while ago which I would like to quote:
As for us in Kimberley, we continue to struggle along trying to rim a unit of approximately 100 men in the rented lower half of the Oddfellows hall. We continue to hire half of a civilian garage to house our vehicles, and rent rooms in the adjoining public school for training space on parade nights. The total bill to the public for all this is, I know, much more than would be the case in a more efficient plant. We do our best, but the training suffers and the administrative headaches are too numerous to mention.
That was brought to my attention at that time and I wrote to the minister about it, at which time I also presented our case. I received a very nice letter from the minister stating that the question of construction of armouries across Canada was receiving special consideration, and also that the question of an armoury at Kimberley would receive most careful consideration. But at that time he could not justify its construction. I hope now, in view of the fact that I have heard just recently that they were going to construct an armoury in Vancouver that we might divert at least a portion of the funds to constructing an armoury in Kimberley.
In Kimberley we have a wonderful unit. They are a good group of men and they are working very hard to make a success of the militia department in that area. They are using old equipment and their headquarters are now situated in Cranbrook. That means travelling to and fro 20 miles each way on each meeting night which, especially during

the winter months, has created a certain amount of confusion. I am sure that if the armouries were located in Kimberley the unit there would expand and we would have a very wonderful militia organization in that area.
Due to the geographical location of East Kootenay-I believe I brought this up at the estimates committee at the time-we only have one unit in Kootenay East operating at the present time. The suggestion was made that in the case of emergency units would come from Trail or Revelstoke. I would like to bring to the minister's attention that owing to our location it would be practically impossible to get there in time to be of any assistance. I should say that the Kimberley group is using inadequate facilities now at Cranbrook.
Only yesterday I received a wire from the small centre of Creston of about 3,000 people, in which they say they are very anxious to form a militia unit in that area and the request has now been forwarded. They say:
Before leaving Ottawa please inquire as to formation of militia unit here with lease or purchase of buildings and property of Creston Can-ners. Premises have been inspected by department official and understand approved-
I understand that they will be very adequate for a militia unit in the Creston area.
I would like to ask the minister if he would give some consideration to the forming of a unit in Kimberley or the forming of a unit in Creston, and also the construction of adequate headquarters in Kimberley. I feel this has been going along now for a number of years and with the prospect of an excellent unit in Creston and also in Kimberley I believe this support would certainly be of great benefit to the Kootenay East area.

I should like to thank the hon. member for his interest in the militia units in the area. I know the engineering company at Kimberley and I have seen the reports, which confirm what the hon. member has said regarding the efficiency of that unit. I know that the accommodation is hardly adequate. Unfortunately there are no funds in this year's estimates for an armoury in that area, nor were there any funds for an armoury in Vancouver, so I cannot transfer money from Vancouver to Kimberley. But if the hon. member can suggest any better accommodation which might be rented we would be very pleased to look into it. As for a new unit at Creston, we will be very pleased to look into that when the application arrives.

Mr. Chairman, as the headquarters of the artillery battery which the hon. member for Kootenay East spoke of,
Supply-National Defence which is Cranbrook, are in Trail I would like to take this opportunity to briefly bring to the minister's attention the devotion of those who carried on in Trail and Nelson with respect to the artillery unit and the engineer company throughout the years. I would also like to bring to his attention that the armoury at Nelson can still do with some improvements. I want to ask the minister if he could briefly inform the house as to what is the situation now with respect to the militia and civil defence? Actually what part is the militia playing in the civil defence organization at this time?

The part played by the militia in civil defence is similar to that which is assigned to the regular army, as far as reentry operations are concerned, and that is why they are being trained in the duties of rescue work and re-entry operations into areas which may have been destroyed either by enemy action or by some catastrophe.
The militia units are organized into a number of support columns-I think approximately 44 support columns-across the country, where they are organized into various types of units, engineers, medical, signals personnel and reconnaissance companies. They are available to move to any area which is either affected by bombs or by fall-out.

I should like to ask the minister whether there has been an agreement to sell the armouries on University avenue in Toronto to the administration of metropolitan Toronto and, if so, what is the nature of that agreement?

An agreement was reached about two years ago, on a request from the metropolitan area of Toronto, which required the site of the University avenue armouries in connection with the construction of a new courthouse and so forth adjacent to the parliament buildings in the area-
Osgoode Hall.
Yes, Osgoode Hall.

-adjacent to Osgoode Hall, where there is a large municipal development nearby. So we have one armoury I think actually under construction at the present time in the eastern part of Toronto. One will be constructed in the north and one in the west.

May I ask whether it is a fact that the original agreement between the federal government and the city of Toronto for the construction of this armoury, I think in 1897, a year which I remember well because I was born in that year, contained a clause under which the federal government must return to the city of Toronto free of encumbrance the site and title of the University avenue armouries in Toronto at such time as they are no longer required by the Department of National Defence? When that report was received I had the legal officers of the department look into the original agreement and they do not substantiate the claim.
So the minister is quite satisfied on the advice he has received that there is no legal difficulty in the way of this agreement which he has mentioned?
I have so been informed by the legal officers of the department.

May I ask a supplementary question on that. I have noticed even within the last few days that there has been a letter in the Toronto press which indicated that the commanding officers of some of the units still using University avenue armouries as their mess were wondering whether they might continue on. Incidentally I am one who did some training there some years ago.

Tradition dies very hard in the army, as the hon. member knows, and there have been some officers in some of the old units who have disliked the prospect of giving up their old messes which are located in the University avenue armouries and having to move elsewhere. Some of them have thought that there may be greater difficulties with recruiting, but all these factors were very carefully examined and the advice of the militia commanders at the time and the advice of the general officer commanding Toronto was taken into consideration, and as a result of that we found that it would be to the benefit of the militia and would certainly be of great convenience to the ultimate development of the project in the metropolitan area of Toronto.

Like the hon. member for Greenwood I had great sentimental regret at this transtaction, because one afternoon in the early days of the first war, disgusted with my inability to translate a Latin text, I walked down from the university library to University avenue and enlisted in the
[Mr. Pearkes.!

armouries, and I am sorry it is going to disappear. But may I ask another question of the minister. Has there been a proposal made for a provost corps training centre at Elliot Lake, and can the minister give me some information as to what was done about that proposal.

Yes. When the situation in Elliot Lake developed and the economy of the city was disrupted the department was asked to see if it was possible to locate any unit there. At that time we were considering the possibility of establishing the provost corps school elsewhere than at Shilo because the accommodation in Shilo was required for other things. A reconnaissance party of officers went down and looked over the place. They were shown the greatest courtesy by the mining company there and in Toronto where Mr. Winters went to a good deal of trouble to show the type of accommodation that there was. Unfortunately the accommodation was not centralized in any one place but centred at various points and could not be readily made available, so ultimately it was decided in agreement with the mining company and I believe the city authorities that it would not be practicable to establish a school at Elliot Lake.

I did not notice tonight whether the minister answered my question about personnel going to the Congo. I wanted to know what was the number of personnel speaking the French language that was designated to go to the Congo.

I cannot give the actual number of French speaking officers and men who are going, but I did give instructions that wherever possible French speaking officers and men were to be included in the contingent. I understand a number of men from the Royal 22nd regiment have been selected for that duty, they having been trained as signallers. There are French speaking personnel of the royal Canadian corps of signals. I would hazard a guess that at least 50 per cent of the personnel going there are fluent in the French language and that many others have a basic knowledge of the French language.
Could the minister indicate how many of the officers can speak the French language or what proportion can do so?

I cannot give a definite answer, but I would say that approximately 20 out of the 30 are able to speak the French language sufficiently well to be able to discuss their problems with the Belgium authorities or the United Nations authorities who are in the Congo now. I should like a pay a word of tribute to the way in which the officers

of French speaking Canada have responded to this call and have, without exception, expressed their keenness to serve their country-in this way.

Before this item carries I want to bring to the attention of the minister a question that has arisen particularly during the last couple of years. I refer to the difficulty which is sometimes experienced by men leaving the service who find it difficult to obtain employment with the result that in some cases they are unemployed for a number of months although not entitled to receive unemployment insurance benefits. I understand that at one time this matter was considered by the responsible people in the Department of National Defence, and for administrative reasons they recommended against providing some form of unemployment insurance in such cases. Personally, I think it is most unfair, particularly when men happen to be discharged during a period of recession-that is the polite term we use at the present time-and are unable to find employment for some months. I would ask the minister if he has had this matter drawn to his attention. It has been brought to my attention lately both by men who are in the service anticipating their discharge and by others who have been unemployed for some time. Is some consideration being given by the Department of National Defence to recommending to the other departments of government arrangements for the inclusion of servicemen under the Unemployment Insurance Act?
The hon. member speaks of a period of recession. Would he explain that and tell us what he means by it?
By recession I mean that while the Progressive Conservative government is in power there are close to half a million men unemployed in Canada.

I do not think the number of men who are employed or unemployed comes within the scope of this particular vote. However, regarding the payment of unemployment insurance, personnel in the services are not eligible for these benefits, but it should be remembered that when a man's time has expired a certain amount of leave is granted to him according to the length of his service-leave which is accompanied by pay-and again, when he comes out with an honourable discharge at the completion of his service he receives a gratuity.

I wish to direct a question either to the minister or to the associate minister. Can the minister confirm or deny that a letter was sent to camp commanders 79951-0-484
Supply-National Defence telling them that all chemicals were henceforth to be bought from a specific firm in Vancouver?

I have no knowledge of this. It seems to me that all chemicals are bought through the Department of Defence Production. I do not know why there would be any chemicals bought through other channels unless the quantity involved was very small and had to be obtained locally.
Does the minister deny that this matter was brought to his attention and that a second letter was sent out with instructions to ignore the first one?
I cannot deny or confirm that. I have no recollection of it, and I cannot say whether such a letter was sent out. You have probably got a copy of it.

I want to thank the minister, first of all, for the answers he gave to my questions about the infra-red equipment and the navigational aids for tanks. I am pleased to note that development is proceeding along those lines and that this kind of equipment has now reached the testing stage.
The minister also told us that one of the roles of the brigade groups in Canada would be to deal with commando raids. Enemy commando raids are usually made either to secure information or to knock out installations. We have many installations, communications and radar systems or warning systems which are in very isolated places in the Arctic or in coastal areas which are not easily reached by aircraft. The minister intends to provide our troops with Bobcats, but these would possibly not give the kind of mobility which he would need in a situation of that kind.
We have heard a great deal about these hovercraft which travel on a cushion of air, and it would seem that a vehicle of this kind would be ideal for recovering troops which might have to be parachuted into isolated areas to deal with any commando raids that might take place. Would the minister tell us if any consideration is being given to the acquisition of vehicles of this kind for our armed forces?

The vehicle to which the hon. gentleman refers has not yet been fully developed. Naturally the department is watching the progress of that development with great interest. I think it will be a couple of years yet before this particular type of vehicle becomes operational. If I recall correctly, money has been voted for the development; some $2.5 million has been contributed by the government toward the development of this Avro car project.

Supply-National Defence
At the present time we are relying upon helicopters. We also have the Otter aircraft, and we also have the Cansos which are now being replaced by the Albatross which will be an infinitely better aircraft and capable of landing on water in those areas.
Reference was made to the commando type of operation, and I did not reply to that. It is possible that commando type operations in conjunction with air attacks on this continent might be undertaken, and in order to be prepared for any eventuality we do have troops trained for operations in the Arctic.
While I am on my feet, I should like to thank the hon. member for the discourse he gave this afternoon on psychological training. We shall be pleased to study that carefully and look fully into his recommendations.
I wonder if the minister could say if the army has adopted the United States radiac meter CDV-710 model 5 and if it has yet obtained delivery?
I do not think we have had supplies in quantity as yet.
Is this not the basic equipment necessary for testing drinking water and food for radioactive contamination?
I believe that is one of the uses which the equipment is designed to serve.

I wonder if the minister could say if the army has ordered the IM-108? Can the hon. gentleman say if the army has bought this piece of equipment, whether the contract is let to a United States firm, whether the contract is still in force or whether it has been cancelled?
The contract for that type of equipment is let through the Department of Defence Production. I would not be able to inform the hon. member whether it has actually been let.
Could the minister say if the army has any of this basic equipment necessary for civil defence and survival operations sufficient to issue to its units concerned?
At the request of the hon. gentleman I placed before the committee on defence expenditures a full list of the equipment which was being obtained.

Mr. Chairman because of the lack of the necessary equipment in that list I was really wondering whether the minister had managed to obtain enough in the meantime, or whether we are still, you might say, defenceless in respect of this basic equipment for civil defence?

No, we certainly are not defenceless as far as civil defence equipment is concerned. We have a large quantity on order and as funds become available and as the equipment becomes available we are obtaining some.

Item agreed to.
223.	Construction or acquisition of buildings, works, land and major equipment, $70,410,000.

For two years the Department of National Defence has been developing an amphibious vehicle known as the Bobcat in conjunction with the Canadian Car Company of Fort William. On several occasions I have asked the minister about the progress being made in the development of the vehicle, and whether a decision has been reached to adopt this vehicle for the Canadian army. I am particularly interested in this program because the Canadian Car Company would in all likelihood be the successful contractor by reason of the fact that this vehicle was designed in their shops. Therefore I was very much interested to hear the minister say in his opening remarks yesterday that the Bobcat is still under active consideration. If the final report shows that the vehicle comes up to expectations it will then be possible for the government to order production. Assuming that the department responsible for the recommendation makes a favourable report can the minister inform the committee as to the number of vehicles that would be produced?

As I said a few minutes ago, the vehicle is in the final stages of its development. When that development has been completed, if the decision is taken by the government to acquire this vehicle, as I certainly hope it will be if it comes up to expectations, then we shall go into production. At the present time it is too early to say exactly how many we should require, but it would be in the order of the magnitude of a couple of hundred or more.

Is the minister in a position to say something about the challenge and the practicability of the development of the Canadian armed forces of air cushion vehicles of the sort which are proving themselves in the United States and in the United Kingdom? If supported in doing so I am sure there are several Canadian companies capable even yet of developing such a vehicle. I should like to hear from the minister whether the Department of National Defence has given any particular consideration to this air cushion vehicle?

Yes; that is precisely the question I answered about five minutes ago. I explained that we are watching with interest the development of the so called Avro car. The development which is going on in the United Kingdom, on the isle of Wight, is known as the hovercraft. I inspected that personally last year. Of course, they are still in the very early stages of development and none of them is proven as yet.

One more question; some time ago I asked about the government's intention as to the purchase of 1,000 prefabricated homes to be used by army personnel. Can the minister now indicate whether there has been a major decision in the matter as yet?
No decision has been made in that matter. It is not clear what the requirement will be.

Mr. Chairman, with reference to item 223, concerning construction and acquisition of buildings, some time ago I presented to the Minister of National Defence a brief concerning the proposed construction at Kitchener, Ontario, of a north Waterloo defence building. Such a structure would accommodate the following garrisons now located in various buildings where facilities are inadequate: 54th L.A.A. regiment, Scots Fusiliers of Canada; the 48th field squadron, Royal Canadian Engineers; 137th company Royal Canadian Army Service Corps; 12th medical company Royal Canadian Army Medical Corps; Kitchener detachment 18th militia group headquarters; R.C.N. Kitchener to H.M.C.S. Star; army recruiting office, regular forces; navy recruiting office, regular forces; headquarters Ontario region No. 3 civil defence; Waterloo county headquarters No. 3 civil defence. Existing accommodation in these cases, as mentioned in the brief, are not too satisfactory. As an honorary member of both of these units, I understand some of these problems.
Advantages of the proposed national defence building are many and are outlined in various items in the brief presented. If these garrisons were housed in one building they would be better equipped to co-operate in peace as well as during an emergency, and would contribute to the efficiency, cooperation and good morale of all military forces.
Such a building would bring to the public a proper perspective of the role of our military and civil defence forces in the preservation of our way of life. It would create pride in service and pride of unit for the serving militiamen and a feeling of recognition for civil defence forces. The building would enhance the efforts of service information 79951-0-iSii
Supply-National Defence branches to attract the right type of man into the permanent forces and would induce the general public to take an interest in civil defence and to attend lectures to study survival, rescue and first aid techniques.
The substantial economy possible by the erection of such a building compared with the present facilities is well known to the department. These garrisons, under their commanding officers, are doing a splendid work. I hope the minister will give this matter his very serious consideration.

Item agreed to.
Royal Canadian Air Force-
224.	Operation and maintenance, $536,737,000.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether the minister can give me some information about the equipment situation about the CF-100? I fancy the CF-100 is a plane which is not being manufactured now. It is still in use both in Europe and in Canada. What is the reserve situation? How long can we go on like this without manufacturing the CF-100 to keep the CF-100 squadrons in operation?

The situation regarding the CF-100 is that there are quite a large number of these aircraft in reserve, and they have been rotated between the active squadrons and the reserve. It has not yet been necessary to cannibalize any of them; that is taking parts of one to put in another. We have sufficient spare parts for the time being and I think sufficient parts to carry on during the life of the aircraft. We expect the aircraft to be phased out in 1962.
With respect to the figure of $170 million which he referred to earlier as being expended for military air transport, can the minister say to which year he was referring, 1959-60 or 1960-61?
That is the total amount for the acquiring of the aircraft to which I referred. Did I say it was included in this year?
Yes.
That was incorrect. It is the total amount to complete the purchase of the aircraft to which I referred.

Can the minister estimate how many additional transport aircraft he could obtain if the Canadian government divested itself of the responsibility for the SAGE-Bomarc program and the $120 million was used alternatively for the purchase of transport aircraft?

Supply-National Defence
There are 12, 106's, 10, 109's, 4, 130's, 10, Albatross, 4 of the new Caribou and 25 Otters.

I think the minister misunderstood my question. Can he estimate how many aircraft of the standard type of air transport he could obtain for the additional $120 million if the government should divest itself of the responsibility for the SAGE-Bomarc program or spent that same amount of money obtained from elsewhere?

The average price of a larger transport would be about $4 million. I wish to emphasize again that the SAGE project is not restricted to the use of the Bomarc. If the Bomarc is not proceeded with we would still go ahead with SAGE so that interceptors could operate effectively over Canadian air space. Whether they were United States interceptors or our own Canadian interceptors they would require the SAGE environment system.

If it was only being used by United States interceptors presumably there is no reason why, if they needed it, they should not pay for it. Can the minister tell us whether lists of R.C.A.F. personnel have been supplied to any private commercial firms for commercial purposes? I have a letter here and I think the minister has a similar letter or a copy of the same letter from someone in Edmonton alleging that a list of R.C.A.F. personnel had been given to a private moving company in Edmonton.

Not that I know of. The situation regarding personnel moving from one station to another is that each station receives from the industry the names of reliable companies which are recommended for the movement of the household effects of personnel. The serviceman is then informed that from this list of well known companies which have proved to be reliable he may select any one firm that he likes. If, on the other hand, he decides to ignore the list and to use a form of transportation the costs of which are in excess of those that are normal for the movement he is then expected to pay the difference.

I recognize that old and continuing policy, but there is an allegation in this letter that lists have been supplied to a moving company which in turn wrote to airmen in the Edmonton district. If I give this letter to the minister at some future time will he look into the matter?
I will be very pleased to do so.

Would the minister indicate
the policy with respect to Trans-Canada Air

Lines pilots being allowed to participate in auxiliary squadrons of the Royal Canadian Air Force? Is there a limitation on the percentage of T.C.A. pilots who can participate in any squadron and, if so, why?

Yes, there is a limitation on the number of pilots for the obvious reason that we would not wish to have too many pilots from these important commercial companies serving with the auxiliary squadrons.
Has the percentage allowed been reduced recently and, if so, did the minister consider the previous allotment excessive?
I do not think the actual percentage has been reduced yet but there has been an indication that there will be a lower percentage in the future.
Is there any intention that they should be excluded altogether from the auxiliary squadrons? I would hope that is not the case and I should like to have the minister's assurance.
As long as the auxiliary squadrons are in operation and are included in the establishment of the air force reserve, the pilots to whom the hon. member has referred will not be excluded entirely.

In the minister's very careful statement which he gave tonight in closing the debate on the administration item, for which we thank him, he mentioned a figure of three interceptors in lieu of each Bomarc missile. Would the minister elaborate on that? I remember that at the time of the controversy in the United States General Kuter said that in the event the Bomarc squadrons were cancelled he would want one interceptor to replace each missile and there was some question whether that might not be excessive because interceptors can fly more than one sortie.
It was three to one in capital cost and in operation and maintenance expenses.
In giving the ratio of three to one the minister referred to cost rather than aircraft?
That is correct.
That would be on the basis, no doubt, of the cost remaining to be paid after the preliminary development costs had been written off.
Yes.
Item agreed to.
225.	Construction or acquisition of buildings, works, land and major equipment, $228,192,000.

Mr. Chairman, I attended some 26 meetings of the special committee on defence expenditure. I have listened very intently to everything that has been said by the Minister of National Defence and the Associate Minister of National Defence, and thus far I have not heard any convincing arguments as to any benefit that can accrue to Canada from the installation of the Bomarc. I am not going to take up the time of the committee in repeating the arguments that I put forward in the special committee on defence expenditures. I am not going to repeat the arguments I used last night or this afternoon because they are well known to the house. I am just going to say that in my opinion this is a bad policy, a waste of public money, and will in no way prove of benefit in the defence of Canada. Because I believe in having the courage of my convictions, I move, therefore:
That vote 225 of the national defence estimates be reduced by $8 million, the approximate amount allocated for Bomarc installation expenditures for the fiscal year 1960-61.
For the reasons I have already given, we cannot accept this amendment.

Mr. Chairman, this, in effect, is the same amendment that this party moved earlier in the session when we were considering interim supply. For that reason, sir, you may wish to consider whether or not it is in order, a decision having been taken at that time. If you decide it is in order, for the sake of consistency and in view of the statements we have made that we believe this program does not involve the best possible use of the Canadian taxpayers' money in the defence field, we would have to support the amendment.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member did not raise formally a point of order? Is the committee ready for the question?
Amendment (Mr. Winch) negatived: Yeas, 21; nays, 35.

Earlier tonight the minister said that the Bomarc sites were so small he felt it would not be likely they would be vulnerable to a missile launched three or four thousand miles away. I wonder if he would elaborate on that a little bit, especially in view of the information he gave to the select committee which would indicate an intercontinental ballistic missile launched even six or eight thousand miles away and carrying a five-megaton warhead would knock
Supply-National Defence out a Bomarc station even if it missed by its maximum rate of error of a full two miles.

The area of the site is not extensive. It would only be a few acres which would cover the actual positions of the launchers. I think it would be extremely difficult for a missile which was launched, shall we say, from Russia, to have the accuracy necessary to hit one of these sites. Now, it is not impossible. Nothing is impossible. Perhaps as missilry development continues it may be possible that they could be hit, but at the present time I think it would be very unlikely.

I do not wish to labour this, and I am also sure the minister would not wish inadvertently to create any wrong impression. Surely he is not arguing that an intercontinental ballistic missile carrying a five-megaton warhead, and which came within a mile and a half or two miles of a Bomarc site, would not put that site out of operation, when the sites are soft and do not have hardening.
There will be a certain amount of hardening around these sites. I question whether a missile landing at the distance the hon. member suggests would necessarily disrupt the launching pads.

I do not wish to quarrel with the minister, but the chart he showed us in the special committee indicated that there would be total destruction for a radius far beyond that, and certainly the personnel on the site would be killed.
As I said, there is a certain amount of hardening being done around these sites, that is to some of the installations which will be below ground.

Item agreed to.
Defence research and development-
Defence research board-
226.	Operation and maintenance, $23,952,119.

I have some correspondence from some people in Edmonton. I am not going to read it because I can paraphrase it. They are concerned about the activities of the Suffield laboratory, which were dealt with by the minister in answer to a question I asked last session. The minister suggested that the experiments were of a purely defensive nature. They ask, would it not be proper for the station to be under civilian and not military control. They say there is a very close guard kept all around the station and that the personnel working there are required to sign declarations not to divulge the type of research being conducted. A number

Supply-National Defence of people are of the opinion that this work is of an offensive, anti-social, anti-humanitarian character. I would ask the minister if he would just inform the committee if the research at Suffield is purely of a defensive nature and not concerned with the manufacture of those insects and other things which cause great damage to life and which one United States military expert said were much cheaper than nuclear weapons. Does the minister think it would be advisable to bring this establishment under civilian control in order to allay these fears as to the type of research being conducted?

Do the hon. member's correspondents suggest that there is a member in this house for the constituency of Medicine Hat, in which this station is located, and that he might have some knowledge of what is going on there?
We admit it, but he does not say anything about it.

The head of the Suffield experimental station is a civilian, Mr. Penny. This whole project comes under the defence research board, which is composed of civilians. There are perhaps some military personnel employed there in connection with administrative and guard duties. The organization and running of that station is under Mr. Penny, a civilian, and I believe the staff of scientists is composed of civilians.
Now, in so far as the other parts of the question are concerned, I may say I visited Suffield last fall. I can assure the hon. gentleman from personal inspection that all the experiments which are carried out there are of a purely defensive nature. If they are connected with chemical or bacteriological work, it is to see how the livestock, our crops and our people can be protected against that type of warfare. There is no manufacturing of chemical gases or anything of that nature carried out at that station, other than very small quantities which may be required for tests. But as some of the chemicals used are of a very dangerous nature, if people who are not protected came near those areas it is necessary for the guards to prevent them from moving through the area. The vital parts of the area are all wired off by security fences.
Mr. Chairman, I am very pleased to have this clear and detailed explanation from the minister and I shall inform my correspondents of his answer.

Item agreed to.
National defence general-
230. To authorize, notwithstanding section 30 of the Financial Administration Act, and subject to

allotment by the treasury board, total commitments of $2,950,656,748 for the purposes of the foregoing votes relating to national defence, regardless of the year in which such commitments will come in course of payment (of which it is estimated that $1,420,466,950 will come due for payment in future years), $1.

Mr. Chairman, I have a question which I think should perhaps more properly have been asked on item 221 but I wonder if the minister would accept my question under the heading of "national defence general"?
My question has to do with destroyer-escorts, and I was wondering whether the minister would consider answering whether construction of the escorts has been started yet, whether any have been completed, and at what shipyards has the construction taken place?

The construction of the six repeat Restigouche has started on all six ships. You asked for the location. The construction of the MacKenzie was commenced in October, 1958 by Canadian Vickers Limited of Montreal. That was the pilot vessel of this type. The Saskatchewan is being constructed at the Victoria Machinery Depot and that contract is being split between the Victoria Machinery Depot and Yarrows Limited, both of Victoria, British Columbia. Construction commenced in August, 1959.
With regard to the Yukon, construction commenced in October, 1959, at the Burrard Drydock Company Limited of North Vancouver. Regarding the Qu'Appelle, construction started in January, 1960 at the Davie Shipbuilding Limited yard at Lauzon, Quebec. Regarding the Annapolis, construction was started by the Halifax Shipyard, Halifax, Nova Scotia, in April, 1960. In regard to the Nipigon, construction was started in July, 1960 by Marine Industries Limited, Sorel, Quebec.
When does the minister expect that these ships will be in operation?
I think it takes about four years to complete the construction and the tests, and it would be approximately that length of time before they came into operation.

This item is the one which enables the government to make advance commitments with respect to the equipment it is buying and I would like to very briefly at this time again caution the government and raise the question which I have raised before in the committee.
Tonight we are being asked to authorize expenditures of $1.6 billion for the armed forces of Canada, but in addition to that we are being asked to commit the government

and the people of Canada to a further expenditure of hundreds of millions of dollars for future equipment.
We were very appreciative of the minister's statement earlier this evening. It contained more information by far than his earlier statement, when we would have expected it. He made a reasoned attempt to deal with some of the problems that we have raised, and as a matter of fact his answer underlined in stark detail the uneasiness which we have in respect to some of the policies of the present government. I do not wish to recapitulate at the present time all the points which have been dealt with. I made notes of some of them; but I have just made a resolution not to rehash them all again tonight.
But I would like to take this opportunity to say that what we have proposed is not a negative policy. It is not a policy of merely disengaging from the use of nuclear arms for Canadian forces on Canadian soil, and from the use of atomic offensive weapons with the air division overseas. It is not just being dissatisfied with certain pieces of equipment that the present government intends to secure for the armed forces of Canada. It is a change of direction and a change of emphasis. It is a warning to the government to consider at this point, before it spends any further and before it becomes involved in greater detail and in greater capacity in new projects, the rejection of spending on defensive weapons for use in an all-out nuclear war which would be useless under those conditions and which would not in fact provide a defence under those circumstances.
I am sure that the minister will agree that he has a real problem. He himself told us, I think this afternoon-if I remember correctly-that it would not be too long before the Russians would have several hundred intercontinental ballistic missiles. Once that condition is reached the possibility of widespread construction is very great indeed.
Under these circumstances, Mr. Chairman -as we have tried to point out during this debate-conventional defensive weapons, if that is what you want to call them, even with atomic warheads as presently in existence, or as presently contemplated, are ineffective. They just will not do the defensive job which should be done.
Under these circumstances we feel the change of direction that we have suggested is one which will take this money, which we feel would otherwise be wasted, and direct it into equipment and into those aspects of defence which would contribute to peace through the mechanics of stopping brush
Supply-National Defence fires or limited situations before they develop into an all-out thermonuclear war- because this is our only hope as far as defence is concerned.
If any of these situations get out of hand and thermonuclear war does develop, then the limited amount we have spent on defence and the limited defences we have will be, if not useless, virtually useless to us. Therefore, it is for this reason that I would ask the government to pause in its course to take a look at the direction in which it is going; a direction which some of us feel is not too different a direction from that of national defence policy of three years ago, at which time the first sputnik had not been put into orbit and the threat of massive attack by intercontinental ballistic missiles seemed still to be very far in the future.
We ask the government to ponder on these things and to consider if now is not the time to change the course of Canadian defence policy so as not to waste further funds on inadequate weapons which will not provide real defence, even though they may be represented as providing some defence; but rather to put our limited resources into those things which will be helpful, which will supply the flexibility and the opportunity for coping with situations which if they got out of hand might break the peace and bring on a thermonuclear holocaust.

I can assure the hon. member that the Minister of National Defence and the Associate Minister of National Defence and their advisers, military and civil, are very conscious of the responsibility which has been placed on their shoulders and they will do their best to ensure that the money which is made available to them for national defence is used to the very best advantage, and we shall take cognizance of and consider the recommendations which have been made by the hon. member.

Mr. Chairman, I have a question under this item. I am not sure if I am quite in order, but I am so seldom out of order that I trust the committee will not criticize me. It has been brought to my attention that owing to the numbers of members of the armed forces in Halifax there is quite a lot of competition between civilians and military personnel in housing and the cost of housing is unusually high in that city. I was asked at the request of a member who is unfortunately not with us tonight to ask the minister if he has had any complaints concerning this situation and if the department would consider, if they are going to continue their present naval program, the undertaking of a housing project for the naval forces in order to relieve this situation.
7666	HOUSE OF
Supply-Trade and Commerce

Mr. Chairman, we are fully aware of the shortage of housing for service personnel in the Halifax area. We have under consideration at the present time the erection of a considerable number of additional houses for married quarters. It is unfortunate that in a city like Halifax where there is a large congregation of service personnel there is no adequate civilian accommodation to enable the servicemen to live out in rented quarters.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I propose dealing with some aspects of the Department of Trade and Commerce. I shall not make any attempt to cover all the points in such a wide ranging department, but as we reach various items in the estimates questions may be asked and answers given at those points.
I would direct hon. members to the annual report of the department which for the second year in succession has been issued in somewhat new form and gives in part I a review of economic and trade developments with regard to this country. Part II deals with the work of the department in detail.
The remarks which I have to make tonight are divided into four main sections. I will speak about certain organizational changes which have been taking place in the department. I will deal with trade promotion activities of the department, and with general trade policy, and conclude with a review of our present trade position and the outlook for the balance of the year 1960.
As new programs develop and as the emphasis in our operation changes to meet new situations it has been found essential to modify the organizational establishment of the department and over the past year a number of important organizational changes have occurred. Some of these were initiated by a highly respected member of the civil service of Canada, the late John English, who was deputy minister of the department a year ago and after a lengthy illness passed away on January 1 of this year. He had spent 33 years with the Department of Trade
[Mr. Herridge.l

and Commerce. Mr. English's devotion to duty and his professional skill were appreciated by all of us who knew him.
I owe a great deal to the experience and advice of the late John English. I found him a most devoted public servant and a man who had great capabilities and a love for his work, and he had a friendly disposition toward all those with whom he came in contact. His death at the age of 58 was a tragic loss to his associates and to the business community of Canada.
Early last year reorganization of the department was undertaken for greater efficiency and to provide the maximum of assistance to Canadian businessmen. In June, 1959 the area divisions of the trade commissioner service and the international trade relations branch were integrated. As a result a number of trade commissioners are now receiving experience in trade policy matters and the trade relations branch has been brought into export development as well as trade policy work. This move, coming at a time when trade policy negotiations have assumed a role of crucial importance with respect to our export trade, has been well received in the department and by businessmen.
In May of this year arrangments were made to recruit two new assistant deputy ministers to assume responsibility for the department's activities with respect to domestic commerce and commodity services. Interdepartmental competitions have been held and the new officials will take office shortly. The department is placing increased emphasis on its promotional activities in Canada. Every effort will be made to uncover new opportunities for industrial development and to create a climate in which these opportunities can be translated into action.
When the present organization changes are fully effective the Department of Trade and Commerce will comprise four major areas of responsibility. Each of these will be assigned to an officer of assistant deputy minister rank reporting to the deputy minister. These areas are as follows.
1.	External trade promotion, which has under it the trade commissioner service, the Canadian government exhibition branch and the trade publicity branch.
2.	Trade policy, which has under it the economics branch, the international trade relations branch and the foreign aid services branch.
3.	Commodities and industry, having under it the commodities branch and the agricultural and fisheries branch.

4.	Domestic commerce, which comprises the industrial development branch, the standards branch and the small business branch.
The dominion bureau of statistics, through the dominion statistician continues to report directly to me.
This new organization will improve administrative efficiency and will offer businessmen and exporters a more logical and convenient structure to deal with. We expect that it will also permit the deputy minister and his assistants to devote more time to planning and policy matters.
Now I turn to trade promotion. The promotion of Canada's foreign trade is the purpose for which the department was originally established in 1887. The branches which contribute to this work devote their entire time and energy to serving Canadian businessmen. In this day to day work they employ a full range of techniques for developing foreign trade. They select from the available variety of methods those techniques best suited to any one market at any one time. The department keeps all techniques under review and is constantly alert to adapt them as changing circumstances require.
One technique that has been consistently used to advantage is participation in foreign trade fairs. The department, with the active support of industry, participates in trade fairs in order to sell Canadian goods and services. It has demonstrated that this is an effective means of trade promotion.
The department extends assistance to private industry by ensuring that up-to-date answers on trade fair questions are available; by organizing collective exhibits and bearing part of the costs; and by providing the experienced co-operation of the trade commissioner on the spot, who will do all he can to ensure a successful participation. Results may be direct, as evidenced by immediate contracts completed at the exhibit, or indirect, in terms of transactions conceived at the exhibit but completed long afterward. The firm prepared to recognize trade fair participation as an important though not isolated step in the market development campaign will likely be successful. The 1960-61 program involves some 16 participations. Each individual trade fair participation has been carefully selected for its trade promotion potential and will be carefully exploited.
One example of the varied approaches being developed by the department is in trade fair work in the engineering field. This specific endeavour has been directed to the competitive U.S. market. The first time the department participated in a specialized industrial show was in September 1958. The results were so encouraging that in 1959 we
Supply-Trade and Commerce participated in three additional shows, and this year we are again participating in four shows. It is difficult to estimate the actual dollar value of orders received which are directly attributable to participation in these shows. However, impressive sales in such a variety of equipment as hydraulic attachments for metal working machines, multicavity moulds, vulcanizing equipment, electronic devices, and hydraulic landing gear for aircraft can be credited to such participation. This effort has resulted in increased prestige for the Canadian companies concerned; it has increased the confidence of these firms in their products; and it has proved that there is a significant market in the United States for Canadian manufactured products.
Another effective technique in trade promotion is the trade mission. The department has in the past made occasional use of this technique with success. We believe that the time is particularly advantageous now for this type of promotion to be used in several areas to facilitate greater effort on the part of Canadian business. These conclusions are reinforced by the increased competition in international markets. We have, therefore, embarked on a vigorous new program of trade missions. The department appreciates that to ensure their success the trade missions should be specialized in their objectives. These missions should consist of a small group of enterprising businessmen who will be accompanied by a senior official of the department. Their itineraries will be carefully prepared and co-ordinated through the trade commissioners in the areas concerned.
The department now is developing plans for a number of missions for specific purposes in selective markets. The liberalisation of the British import market has made it possible for exporters of foodstuffs to look again to that market as the substantial outlet they found there before the war. The department therefore proposes to send a mission representative of the Canadian processed food industry to the United Kingdom at the time of the British food fair in London in September. The mission will visit other main centres and have many interviews with the trade.
As a result of the experience gained at previous exhibits where Canadian timber and timber products were features we feel that a trade mission consisting of representative Canadian timber and plywood exporters can do an effective follow-up job to revive interest in Canadian lumber in the United Kingdom. We anticipate that this mission will commence its activities by attending the Manchester building trades exhibition in October.
As part of our program to maintain and develop our trade in the European economic community we are proposing to send

Supply-Trade and Commerce a strong mission representing chemical, metal and mineral, and pulp industries to those six countries in October.
Opportunities for the export of a wide range of technological services to many parts of the world have grown remarkably in recent years. The great fund of experience which we possess in this field as a result of our own rapid economic development opens new and promising avenues to explore abroad. Canadian consulting engineering firms have already secured large contracts and earned excellent reputations in several continents. Attractive opportunities are developing in South America. Up to the present few Canadian firms have acquired first hand knowledge or experience of operations in this area. To meet this need the department is planning a mission of Canadian consulting engineers which will visit selected South American countries in September.
Yet another aspect of trade promotion involves facilitating visits to Canada by businessmen from abroad. The success that can be achieved by encouraging the importers of other countries to come here was demonstrated earlier this year by the visit of a delegation of Rumanians headed by the Rumanian vice minister of agriculture. While in this country they purchased a substantial quantity of livestock and other agricultural products. Included in their purchases of livestock were 110 head of pure bred Holstein-Friesian cows and three bulls, 20 head of Aberdeen Angus cattle, over 1,100 head of Hereford cattle, 200 head of Landrace hogs, and a few sheep. They also purchased a substantial quantity of hybrid seed corn and some soybean seed. It is felt that the purchases will result in further business with Rumania. Departmental officers assisted in arranging the visit of this delegation and also provided assistance while the group was in Canada.
These trade missions represent an important aspect of our new program through which we hope to give still further assistance and encouragement to Canadian exporters in their efforts to maintain and expand markets abroad.
No part of the department has been a greater proponent of the usefulness and value of personal visits to overseas markets than the trade commissioner service, the overseas arm of the department. This field force is continuously at the service of Canadian businessmen engaged in, or interested in engaging in international trade. By September of this year the trade commissioner service will have a total of 63 posts staffed by 114 career officers. In 1939 there were 35 posts and 61 officers. Twenty years ago Canada was represented by trade commissioners in 27

countries; by September of this year our representatives will be in 49 countries.
Three new offices have been established this calendar year, in Glasgow, Canberra and Moscow. A fourth is being opened in the fall at Lagos, Nigeria. The department continues alert to the need for yet further officers and certain other possible new posts are under study.
On the subject of trade policy, although I dealt at some length with this in the debate we had in the house in March, I felt it wise to review the situation again. There has been a good deal of debate both within and outside the house regarding the implications of recent developments particularly in Europe so far as Canada's trade policy is concerned.
There has been a good deal of debate regarding the implications of recent developments, particularly in Europe, for Canada's trade policy. As I indicated to the house last March, our trade policy has been directed to the achievement of a trading system in which Canadian exports have access to markets'- throughout the world on a basis of equality with all other suppliers.
While the trade rules embodied in the general agreement on tariffs and trade are not without imperfections, the principles of most favoured nation treatment and non-discrimination on which this agreement is based provide the kind of trading arrangements best suited to safeguard Canada's diverse and broad trading interests.
The achievement of this multilateral system and the realization of the advantages which would reasonably be expected from it was, for many years, frustrated by the prevalence of severe foreign exchange difficulties in many parts of the world. More recently, with the improvement in world economic and financial conditions, the import controls which have been maintained by many other countries against our goods have been rapidly disappearing. As a result Canadian exporters are for the first time since the war in a position to compete on equal terms in most markets with other most favoured nation suppliers.
While we have come a long way toward the realization of the goal which Canada has been pursuing in the post-war period, more remains to be done. With the progress in the removal of balance of payments restrictions on trade the restrictive effect of widespread agricultural protectionism has become increasingly apparent. The degree of restrictions maintained against imports of agricultural products by other countries seriously affects Canada's trade and disturbs the balance of advantage between the agricultural exporting countries and their trading partners.
While it would be unrealistic to expect that national measures to support agriculture

could be eliminated, there is scope for a significant downward adjustment in the level of agricultural supports and the degree of protection afforded by tariff and non-tariff barriers to trade in agricultural products. I am speaking here of our trading partners abroad. A special examination of this subject has been undertaken in the GATT with a view to finding ways and means of ensuring more reasonable access to world markets for the products of Canada and other agricultural exporting countries.
Our trade policy objectives must, of course, be considered in the light of the emergence of new trading arrangements, particularly in Europe. The six countries of the European economic community

Belgium, France, Germany, Italy, Netherlands and Luxembourg -are proceeding with the setting up of a common market among themselves, looking to economic integration and close political association. These arrangements will eventually involve the elimination of tariffs and quantitative restrictions on trade within the area and the development of a single tariff against imports from outside countries. The first steps in the implementation of these arrangements have already been taken.
In addition, the common market countries are in the process of working out a common agricultural policy. The United Kingdom and the other European countries not members of this common market are establishing an industrial free trade area among themeslves. In the implementation of their E.F.T.A. the United Kingdom and other countries concerned have taken the first step in the elimination of tariff barriers to trade within the area. As a result of these developments two regional groupings are evolving in Europe. Politically Canada has been sympathetic to the broad objectives of European economic integration. We have, however, been conscious that the emergence of two regional groups in Europe could lead to a serious trade split and adversely affect the close trade and economic co-operation which has been established between the European countries and between them and their outside trading partners, including, of course, Canada and the United States.
Canada's direct trade interest in relation to the European economic community is to obtain fair and reasonable access to the common market for Canadian exports. The level of the common market tariff is of critical importance in this respect. Further, some 40 per cent of Canada's exports to the common market countries are agricultural products and the kind of agricultural policy which
Supply-Trade and Commerce is developed by the European economic community will have major significance for the future of Canada's trade and commercial relations with this area.
As far as the free trade area of the seven is concerned, the immediate impact on Canada is the effect on our preferential position in the United Kingdom market. The free trade area arrangements will eventually give the United Kingdom's partners in E.F.T.A. generally the same tariff access Canada now receives in the United Kingdom market. This means that Canada which had previously been accorded preferential treatment in competition with the Scandinavian countries and with Austria, Switzerland and Portugal, will in the future face the prospect of competing with these countries on broadly equal terms in the United Kingdom.
The general agreement on tariffs and trade has been and continues to be the major international instrument for the protection of Canadian interests against possible adverse effects of these regional developments in Europe. Its provisions establish certain criteria and safeguards which must be observed in setting up customs unions of free trade areas. These provisions are useful not only in setting the framework for GATT examination of proposed arrangements but also as the basis for bilateral representations to the countries concerned.
Amongst other important safeguards the GATT requires that in the formation of customs unions or free trade areas participating countries must not raise new barriers to the trade of outside countries. Against these criteria the provisions of the treaty of Rome have been under continuous examination by Canada and the other contracting parties. We have also been active in direct representations and discussions with the six and the European commission.
An important example of our initiative in this regard was the recent consultations with the European economic community concerning the prospective agricultural arrangements of the common market. In these consultations Canada was joined with the United States, Australia, New Zealand and the Argentine. The consultations provided Canada with a further opportunity to remind the European countries of the importance which we attach to the trade in agricultural products and to urge them in the interests of maintaining and developing our mutually advantageous trade to evolve agricultural arrangements which will ensure that Canada has a reasonable opportunity to compete in the European market for agricultural products and to participate in the growth in that market.
