At the recent GATT session the contracting parties had a first opportunity to examine the convention providing for the European free trade association of the seven. These arrangements are to be subject to further GATT examination. Outside the region of Europe there is also the Montevideo treaty signed by Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Mexico, Peru, Paraguay and Uruguay for the establishment of the Latin American free trade association. The terms of this association have also been brought under review in Geneva and will be examined further at the next GATT session this fall.
The forthcoming multilateral tariff conference which opens in Geneva in September will provide an opportunity, in the first phase, for Canada to address itself in negotiations with the E.E.C. countries to the level of the common market tariff. In this respect, the fact that most of Canada's exports to the common market are protected by bound tariff concessions which have been negotiated with the common market countries provides an important safeguard for ensuring continued reasonable terms of tariff access to the European market. To implement the common external tariff member countries of the common market will inevitably be making adjustments in the tariff concessions which they previously negotiated individually. But there is a collective obligation to maintain the general level of reciprocity through entering, as a unit, into new contractual obligations which ensure no less favourable access for outside countries than previously existed. The Canadian government will participate actively in these renegotiations with the common market countries and in the general negotiations to follow.
The tariff conference, in the second phase, will, of course, also provide an opportunity for Canada to negotiate for improved tariff access to other markets throughout the world, including that of the United States.
One further aspect of this tariff conference that is worth emphasizing is that through tariff negotiations between the European seven and common market six the emerging trade split in Europe can be eased. The benefits of all tariff reductions negotiated throughout each phase of the conference will, of course, be extended to Canada and other countries on the basis of the most favoured nation provisions of GATT, including the benefits of the important negotiations between the six and the United States.
Canada is also actively participating in the economic discussions which have been taking place in Paris since the ministerial meetings held there in mid-January last which the Minister of Finance and I attended. At these meetings the 18 European


members of the organization for European economic co-operation and their two associates, the United States and Canada, agreed to proceed with the reconstitution of the O.E.E.C. and established two bodies to deal, in the interim, with certain trade and aid matters, namely the committee on trade problems and the development assistance group.
Canada has been closely engaged in all three endeavours, the first two of which are of special significance in so far as our trade interests are concerned. As the house was informed recently by the Minister of Finance, plans were drawn up at the ministerial meeting in Paris on July 22 and 23 for the establishment of a new organization for economic co-operation and development in which it is envisaged that the European countries, together with Canada and the United States, will participate. The O.E.C.D., as it will be known, is designed to facilitate and promote economic growth and contribute to the development of the world economy and world trade on a multilateral non-discriminatory basis.
With a view to the protection and furtherance of Canada's export interests we are following these matters with the closest attention. The existence of the common market in Europe and of European free trade association are facts of life which must be taken into account. These groupings can develop in ways which will promise larger markets for Canadian goods or, if they take a restrictive turn, our interests could be prejudiced. Our efforts are being directed to ensuring, so far as possible, that outward looking policies will be pursued which will allow us to continue the mutually advantageous trade relationships which have been developed up to this time. The house may be assured that the government is fully aware of the need to keep our trade policy under continuous review in the changing circumstances of today and that our approach to the challenges and new problems of the sixties will be flexible and constructive, bearing in mind our vital trade interests and the need for balance and mutual advantage in the relations with our many trading partners throughout the world.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Thank you very much. I propose now to deal with a review of Canada's trade and the outlook for the next few months. During the past year economic activity in Canada has moved upward in line with expansionary conditions in the world at large. Canada's gross national product is running appreciably above the level of a year ago. Most of this increase reflects a higher volume of physical production; prices have remained fairly stable.
Industrial production is up by 5 per cent in the first five months of this year compared with last. Industries which have contributed to this increase include pulp and paper, base metals, particularly aluminum, nickel and copper, petroleum and natural gas, electric power, asbestos, primary iron and steel, food and beverages, chemicals and a number of the major equipment industries. Despite a further rise in imports of European cars, Canada's output of motor vehicles so far this year has remained a little above the 1959 level.
The over-all growth in business activity has been accompanied by a continuing increase in both wages and profits and in personal incomes generally. More production has in turn created more jobs. Total employment in June and in the first six months of the current year was approximately 2 per cent above the corresponding period of 1959.
Consumer purchasing, though up moderately from a year ago, has not fully kept pace with personal incomes. For several lines of merchandise the disappointing volume of spring sales was attributed, in trade circles, to unfavourable weather. In any event the continuing firm trend of personal income provides underlying strength to the consumer market and indicates that weakness in this sector is apt to be shortlived.
The early year decline in housing starts was the result, in large part, of a general stringency of mortgage funds. However, the level of housing starts was already moving upward by mid-year and this trend will now be reinforced by the broadening of the terms applicable to mortgage loans under the National Housing Act.
In the circumstances described, neither consumer buying nor housing are apt to be a source of further weakening in total demand. On the contrary, both of these market sectors are likely to provide new demand stimulus as the year draws on.
Further encouraging information on economic prospects for the balance of the year has come from the mid-year survey of investment intentions for 1960, the results of which were recently made available in the
Supply-Trade and Commerce report, "Private and public investment in Canada, outlook 1960-mid-year review". The survey indicates that total capital outlays, both private and public, will amount to $8.7 billion in 1960. This figure is little changed from the estimate made early in the year and involves an increase of 4 per cent over actual outlays of $8.4 billion in 1959. The $8.7 billion figure includes a downward revision in the earlier estimate of housing outlays to take account of the relatively low volume of starts in the first half of the year. On the other hand, the mid-year survey indicated an upward revision in the capital spending plans of the business community compared with intentions reported at the beginning of the year. As a result business capital outlays are now expected to be 8 per cent higher in 1960 than in the preceding year. The realization of this program will involve a further increase in activity in construction and related trades and in equipment producing industries in the latter part of the current year.
Apart from its immediate stimulative effects, the continuing high level of plant expansion under way in Canada is a reflection of the confidence with which Canadian business looks to the future. These indications of sustained strength within the domestic economy are reinforced by the continuation of a generally favourable international economic climate. Trade figures for 1960 to date reflect Canada's strong position in foreign markets.
In 1959 the value of Canada's merchandise exports surpassed the $5 billion mark for the first time. In 1960 to date exports are 8 per cent higher than in the same period last year and are running at an annual rate in the neighbourhood of $5.5 billion. This upward movement in exports is taking place in all principal market areas and is widely distributed through most of the major commodity groups.
The expansion in economic activity in the United States over the past year has been accompanied by a further rise in purchases from Canada. Although the business tempo in the United States has moderated somewhat in recent months, there is widespread expectation that the present high level of general activity will be maintained in the period ahead. On this basis Canadian sales to the United States for 1960 as a whole should remain above the previous year's level.
Meanwhile shipments to overseas markets have responded vigorously to the rising level of business activity in most of these countries. In 1960 to date exports to the United Kingdom are up by 20 per cent, to other commonwealth markets by 16 per cent, and to all other countries by 17 per cent.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
A major portion of this growth in exports has consisted of industrial materials. Items such as newsprint, wood pulp, aluminum, nickel, copper and industrial chemicals have been purchased in greater quantities in response to higher business activity in virtually all industrial countries. Despite a reduced volume of housebuilding in the United States, lumber sales in that market have been maintained so far this year and are moving in larger quantities to the United Kingdom and other overseas markets. With Canadian oil now able to move across the border free of restrictions, the export of this commodity, though still below the previous record, is running well above last year's level. A large amount of iron ore is anticipated for the current season. The trend evident in these major items is broadly indicative of the export position of the mineral and forest products groups which together account for nearly two thirds of Canada's exports.
A notable feature of Canada's export position is the expansion under way in sales of manufactured products. Despite a decline in exports of farm implements to the United States, sales abroad of all highly manufactured products taken as a whole have increased by 10 to 15 per cent in 1960 to date. At the same time sales of agricultural products considered as a group have held close to the high level achieved last year.
Just as exports have been expanding to meet the growth in foreign countries, Canadian purchases from abroad have been increasing in response to rising demands in Canada. However, imports have been increasing at a slower rate than exports and in the first five months of the year are up by 4 per cent from the same period of 1959. Shipments from Canadian factories have shown a comparable increase indicating that Canadian manufactured products have been holding their own in the domestic market in over-all terms. Nevertheless, in some lines, producers have encountered severe pressure from import competition. Meanwhile the decline in the external value of the Canadian dollar occurring earlier this year has improved the competitive position of the domestic producers in both home and foreign markets.
The much sharper rise in exports than in imports so far this year has reduced Canada's merchandise trade deficit from $356 million in the January to May, 1959 period to $177 million in the same months of the current year. Indications are that this reduction in the merchandise trade deficit has more than offset the continuing increase in the invisible deficit. This means that the total current deficit on international account is presently


well below the level of a year ago, $318 million in the first quarter of 1960 compared with $415 million in the same period of last year.
A prominent development this year has been the sharp growth in Canada's overseas trade. Exports to and imports from the United Kingdom and the commonwealth as a whole have increased substantially. Exports to other overseas countries taken together have increased markedly whereas imports from this area are a little lower. Canada's trade balance with these countries is therefore increasing, reversing the trend of the previous year.
The substantial growth this year in overseas sales has meant that Canada's exports in the United States, though higher in absolute terms, make up a smaller share of Canada's total exports. Meanwhile the relative importance of the United States as a source of imports has been diminishing for some time. Purchases from the United States are now appreciably lower, in absolute terms, than in 1957 and as a proportion of total imports have declined from 74 per cent in early 1957 to 67 per cent so far in the current year. During this same period Canada's merchandise trade deficit with the United States has been reduced by nearly one half. Even with the growing imbalance on nonmerchandise transactions, Canada's total deficit on current transactions with the United States is $132 million less in the first quarter of 1960 than in the same period three years ago.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I should like to emphasize two points. First, Canada's economic conditions and trade relations are under constant and expert scrutiny. We are increasing the number of senior officers and consolidating the department into an even more efficient and streamlined operation. This will better enable us not only to meet the challenges of today but also to anticipate and minimize the problems of the future.
Second, I cannot stress too much the degree to which a wide range of Canadian products and technical competence are competitive abroad. I offer congratulations to those Canadian businessmen who have ventured so successfully into foreign markets. I hope that their successes will encourage more Canadian firms to look abroad for new sales opportunities. The department stands ready to do all it can to help them.

Mr. Chairman, I should like at the very outset of my remarks to associate myself with the minister in the acknowledgment of the fine public service of his former deputy, the late John English. The remarks that the minister made concerning that

Business of the House
splendid public servant were most appropriate, and I want to express my appreciation to the minister for having made them in his place as minister. The record of public servants like that is something that I think is not always sufficiently appreciated by the people of the country generally and knowing of the splendid work of this former civil servant I want to associate myself with all the words uttered by the minister about him.
Now as to the minister's glowing and enthusiastic picture of the trade situation in Canada, I am afraid I have to take sharp issue with him. I wish it were not so. I wish that the trade picture was as glowing as he indicated. My hope is that some of the hopes he has expressed for it throughout the rest of the year are realized. I do hope that is the case, as I think all hon. members do.
Surely the minister, in presenting a review to the House of Commons of the trade picture of this country, even if it is late at night on the 142nd day of the sitting that this is being done, should not compare the figures on foreign trade representatives in 1960 with those in 1939, because he ought to remember that the country in 1960 about which we are talking has a population of about 18 million persons, and the country of 1939 had a population of about 11 million persons. To compare representation abroad in two such years does not give a very accurate picture.
